He reports a current seizure frequency of 17 per month, typically clustering around periods of sleep deprivation and high work-related stress. component_inputs.note_text:
Department of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Helen Armitage  
Royal London Hospital  
Department of Neurology, Whitechapel Road, London E1 1FR  

Dear Dr Helen Armitage,  

John Smith, DOB: 11-07-1984, Hospital No: S845921 NHS No. 7823495610  
34 Kensington Road, London, W8 5NP 

Diagnoses: 

- Focal epilepsy with focal aware seizures and occasional focal to bilateral tonic-clonic evolution  
- History of childhood febrile seizures (resolved)  
- MRI brain (August 2025): Subtle left mesial temporal sclerosis  
- EEG (July 2025): Interictal left temporal sharp waves  

Current Medication: 

- Levetiracetam 1,000 mg bd  
- Lacosamide 100 mg bd  
- Midazolam 10 mg buccal, as rescue for prolonged seizures (>5 minutes) 

Plan: 

- Optimise anti-seizure medication: increase Lacosamide to 150 mg bd over two weeks if tolerated  
- Continue Levetiracetam 1,000 mg bd  
- Seizure diary to closely track frequency and potential triggers  
- Driving: patient not currently driving; to follow DVLA guidance and remain off driving until seizure-free per regulations  
- Consider referral to the epilepsy surgery MDT if disabling seizures persist despite optimisation  
- Safety advice provided regarding bathing, heights, hot surfaces, and nocturnal supervision  

I reviewed John in clinic today regarding focal epilepsy. He describes brief focal aware seizures characterised by rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu, and transient speech arrest, occasionally followed by right-hand automatisms and, more rarely, progression to bilateral tonic-clonic activity. He reports a current seizure frequency of 17 per month, typically clustering around periods of sleep deprivation and high work-related stress. He has found avoidance of alcohol helpful and is now using a structured sleep schedule. 

There is a remote history of childhood febrile seizures without neurological sequelae. Adult-onset focal seizures began in late 2023. Prior trials included Lamotrigine up to 200 mg bd, which was discontinued due to rash, and Carbamazepine up to 600 mg bd, which reduced frequency but caused significant dizziness and hyponatraemia; both medications were stopped in consultation with his previous team. 

We discussed treatment options. Given the MRI and EEG concordance suggesting a left mesial temporal focus, I have recommended optimising current therapy by titrating Lacosamide to 150 mg twice daily if tolerated, while continuing Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily. He will maintain a detailed seizure diary and track potential triggers. A rescue plan using buccal Midazolam for prolonged seizures was reinforced. 

If disabling seizures persist at a rate similar to the current 17 per month despite dose optimisation and adherence, I will refer him to the epilepsy surgery multidisciplinary team for further evaluation, including consideration of prolonged video-EEG telemetry and neuropsychological assessment. We also reviewed DVLA regulations; he is not currently driving and understands requirements for resumption. 

I will review him again in three months, or earlier if there is any deterioration or adverse effects from the dose increase. 

With best wishes,

component_inputs.note_text:
Epilepsy Centre 

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Maya Thompson  
St George’s Hospital  
Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT  

Dear Dr Maya Thompson,  

Jamie Collins, DOB: 14-02-1992, Hospital No: H839205 NHS No. 9483726150  
12 Willow Close, London, SW18 1AB  

Diagnoses: 

Seizure disorder in the context of learning disability. 

Jamie Collins attended with their carer who assists with communication and seizure logging. The carer reports that seizures are occurring every 2 days on average, based on a written diary and a smartphone log that have been kept consistently since the last review. Seizures are described as sudden behavioural arrest with unresponsiveness lasting 45–90 seconds, occasionally followed by brief confusion. No clear focal features have been captured, and there have been no witnessed injuries. There has been no use of rescue medication since the last appointment. 

Current medications are unchanged since the previous visit. Adherence is reported as good, with doses administered by the carer and a weekly blister pack used to reduce missed doses. No new adverse effects have been noted. Sleep routine has been stabilised and the carer has introduced evening reminders to reduce late dosing. 

Recent investigations: Routine bloods (U&E, LFT, FBC) in August were within reference ranges. The prior EEG was non-specific and did not capture an event. We discussed video capture of typical episodes to aid characterisation; the carer is willing to attempt this where safe. 

Plan: 
- Continue current antiseizure medication regimen as previously prescribed. 
- Maintain the seizure diary and smartphone log to corroborate the current pattern of every 2 days and to record any potential triggers, injuries, or use of rescue medication. 
- Provide short home video of typical events if safe to do so, to assist with further classification. 
- Community learning disability team to continue supporting communication strategies at appointments. 
- Safety advice reinforced around bathing supervision and cooking when fatigued; carer verbalised understanding. 
- We will arrange a follow-up in three months, or sooner if there is any escalation in frequency, prolonged events, or injuries. 

Yours sincerely

This is our first adult clinic review post-transition. From the joint handover summary and today’s history, his typical episodes comprise brief staring spells with eyelid flutter and occasional myoclonic jerks shortly after waking. Generalised tonic–clonic seizures have been infrequent. At present he reports clusters of brief absence episodes every 4 weeks, usually over 1–2 days, often precipitated by reduced sleep and academic stress. No rashes, visual disturbance, or focal neurological symptoms were reported. There is no history of focal onset phenomena. He is not driving.

On examination today he was alert and oriented with normal speech and language. Cranial nerves were intact, tone and power were normal in all limbs, reflexes were symmetric, and coordination and gait were normal. There were no neurocutaneous stigmata.

Paediatric EEGs have shown generalised spike–wave discharges, most recently in 2024. MRI brain (2023) was normal. We will arrange an updated EEG to reassess background and interictal activity in the adult service and to support ongoing management planning. We discussed adherence, regular sleep, and stress management as practical measures that may help reduce breakthrough events. He and his parent were given information on our transition nurse specialist and epilepsy advisor should they wish to discuss education or lifestyle issues further.

I have asked him to keep a simple seizure diary, noting any absence clusters and possible triggers, particularly sleep loss. We will review him in 6 months, or sooner if events increase in frequency, if he experiences any adverse effects, or if a generalised tonic–clonic seizure recurs.

Wendy Brown, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: K482715 NHS No. 6592841037
Flat 7 Brookside Avenue, Newcastle-under-Lyme, ST5 2QD

Diagnoses/summary: Focal epilepsy, likely temporal lobe onset. Marked clinical improvement on current regimen.

Medication history (abridged): Previous exposure to sodium valproate, carbamazepine, levetiracetam, phenytoin, lacosamide, clobazam; mixed tolerability and incomplete control. No history of topiramate or zonisamide use. Currently tolerating dual therapy without notable adverse effects.

Hydration and routine bloods through primary care were acknowledged; no abnormalities reported by the patient.

Plan:
- Continue current antiseizure medications unchanged given sustained benefit and frequency now ≤ once per month.
- Maintain seizure diary and sleep hygiene. Patient to contact the epilepsy nurse if any increase in frequency or new features occur.
- Routine follow-up in 6 months, sooner if breakthrough clusters recur.
- No immediate need for repeat MRI or EEG in view of stability, but will reconsider if clinical pattern changes.

Thank you for your ongoing care of Wendy Brown. Please let me know if there are any concerns in the interim.

Yours sincerely

Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division

Clinic Date: 21 September 2025

Dr Ahmed Khan
Centre for Epilepsy
Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG

Dear Dr Ahmed Khan,

Laura Bennett, DOB: 03-02-1993, Hospital No: H372915 NHS No. 9842136750
Flat 7, 28 Rose Lane, London, EC1A 9AB

Epilepsy

Epilepsy classification: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy (patient reports both generalised and focal seizures)

Background: Post-partum within the last six months with fragmented night-time sleep.

Medication: Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily; Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily. No recent changes reported.

Adherence and tolerability: She reports full adherence using a daily pill organiser. Mild irritability on levetiracetam, otherwise no significant adverse effects. Breastfeeding ongoing; no noted impact from current regimen as per her account.

Seizure history and current pattern: She describes a mixture of focal aware episodes (déjà vu with rising epigastric sensation and brief speech arrest) and generalised tonic–clonic seizures during sleep. Since delivery, frequency has increased in the context of fragmented sleep. Current estimated seizure frequency is 12 to 30 per quarter, with clusters typically following nights of interrupted rest. No injuries, tongue biting occasional, and post-ictal confusion lasting up to 20 minutes after generalised events. No specific auras preceding nocturnal generalised events; focal aware episodes can occur in the evening while settling the infant.

Triggers and contextual factors: Sleep fragmentation and missed naps identified as likely triggers by the patient. She avoids alcohol and reports no intercurrent illness.

Investigations: No recent blood levels requested. Last EEG (prior to pregnancy) reportedly showed generalised spike–wave and left temporal sharp waves, consistent with combined generalised and focal epilepsy. MRI (2019) normal per previous records.

Plan discussed today: We reviewed her current pattern in the post-partum period and the impact of sleep disruption. She wishes to continue breastfeeding and is keen to maintain current medications for now. I have advised seizure and sleep diaries to track correlation with night-time awakenings and will arrange routine bloods (FBC, U&Es, LFTs) for general monitoring. We will book a repeat EEG to reassess interictal changes post-partum. Safety advice discussed regarding nocturnal supervision, recovery position guidance, and avoiding co-sleeping when excessively sleep-deprived, as per standard practice. She understands to seek urgent help if seizures escalate in duration or frequency beyond her usual pattern. We agreed a telephone review in 6 weeks, with earlier contact if concerns arise.

Yours sincerely

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr Amelia Forbes
St Anne’s Family Practice

12 Market Street, Brixton, London SW9 8JQ
Dear Dr Amelia Forbes
Hannah Clarke, DOB: 14-03-1996, Hospital No: H3928471 NHS No. 7419625830
Flat 3, 27 Willow Road, London NW3 1TL 

Diagnoses/summary: Recurrent seizures of uncertain phenotype; post-partum within the last six months with fragmented nocturnal sleep

MRI: No prior brain MRI on record; imaging requested today

EEG: Routine EEG arranged; no previous EEG available for review

Previous medication: None for seizures to date

Not taken: Carbamazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, sodium valproate, topiramate, zonisamide, lacosamide, clobazam, perampanel

Other history: Uncomplicated vaginal delivery five months ago; breastfeeding; no prior neurological history; no head injury; family history negative for epilepsy; mood low at times, likely sleep-related; no illicit drug use; minimal alcohol pre-pregnancy

I reviewed Hannah Clarke in clinic today. She attended with her partner and infant. Since delivery, she describes recurrent events characterised by sudden behavioural arrest, loss of awareness reported by her partner, and brief post-event confusion lasting a few minutes. Some episodes occur out of sleep and others during feeds in the early hours. She reports that the frequency is consistent at seizures twice every 4 days, with clustering around nights following particularly fragmented sleep. There is no clear convulsive activity described, no tongue biting, and no reported incontinence. She has noted a prodromal sense of rising internal anxiety on occasion, but this is not reliable.

She is currently breastfeeding and reports night-time sleep is fragmented due to infant care, with total nightly sleep often below four hours. She has not noticed any specific triggers beyond sleep deprivation. No syncope, no palpitations, no chest pain, and no focal neurological symptoms between events. Blood pressure has been normal post-partum as per community midwife notes.

Examination today was unremarkable: alert, fully oriented, cranial nerves intact, normal tone and power in all limbs, coordination and gait normal. No clinical stigmata of systemic illness. 

Plan:
- Safety advice reinforced, including avoidance of unsupervised bathing and cooking when sleep deprived; advised to avoid co-sleeping during periods of increased event frequency; discussed driving restrictions per DVLA guidance for seizures with impaired awareness.
- Investigations: Routine EEG and MRI brain with epilepsy protocol requested; baseline bloods including FBC, U&E, LFT, calcium, magnesium, glucose, thyroid function; vitamin D as part of general health screen post-partum.
- Management: Discussed treatment options in the context of breastfeeding. She prefers to delay anti-seizure medication until investigations are completed if safe. Given current frequency of seizures twice every 4 days and associated risk, we agreed to expedite tests and arrange an early follow-up within 4–6 weeks; she will consider medication initiation after results. If events escalate or any convulsive seizure occurs, she will contact the service urgently and we will start therapy sooner. 
- Lifestyle: Emphasised sleep optimisation strategies where possible (partner support for one night feed, expressing milk for one feed, daytime rest when feasible). She will keep a detailed seizure diary, including timing relative to sleep and feeds.
- Perinatal considerations: Signposted to perinatal mental health and health visitor support given low mood symptoms; she is open to referral.

I will write with results and see her promptly in review. Many thanks for your ongoing care and support.

Yours sincerely

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Aisha Patel
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr Aisha Patel
Consultant Neurologist,  

Daniel Harris, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: K742118 NHS No. 9076543321  
12 Rowan Close, Brixton, London SW2 1AB

Thank you for your referral and for forwarding the recent employer occupational health summaries, which were helpful as collateral sources alongside the patient’s own account. I reviewed him today in clinic with his partner present. He describes ongoing events occurring roughly weekly, with brief warning symptoms of unease and difficulty focusing, followed by a lapse in awareness noted by colleagues at work and by his partner at home. Observers report that he becomes still, stops responding, and is slow to re‑engage for several minutes. He is generally fatigued afterwards and reports a mild, non-lateralising headache. He denies clear myoclonic jerks or sustained tonic–clonic movements. There has been no clear pattern with sleep deprivation or alcohol, though he reports occasional poor sleep due to shift work. 

The occupational health summaries corroborate a weekly frequency over the past three months, documenting short episodes leading to temporary removal from safety-critical tasks. No injuries have been recorded. He has kept a basic diary that aligns with the employer reports, and his partner has additionally noted two brief nocturnal arousals with confusion but without witnessed convulsions. There is no consistent aura quality beyond the nonspecific warning of unease, and no clear automatisms have been recorded. 

He is currently taking levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily, started by his GP four months ago, with partial improvement in post-event fatigue but no change in the weekly occurrence of events. He is tolerating the medication but feels more irritable; there is no low mood, suicidal ideation, or psychotic symptoms. Neurological examination today was unremarkable. A prior routine EEG from 2023 was reported as normal; we do not yet have the raw data. MRI brain from 2021 was reported as normal per patient; we will request the images and report for review. 

Given the persistently weekly events and limited detail from routine testing, I have advised further characterisation. I will arrange an ambulatory EEG with video and request updated MRI brain epilepsy protocol if prior imaging cannot be retrieved or is inadequate. I have provided written information on seizure first aid and asked him and his partner to continue a detailed diary, including context, duration, recovery, potential triggers, and any observed movements or vocalisations. He consents to us liaising with employer occupational health to synchronise dates and obtain contemporaneous descriptions, as these summaries have been particularly useful. 

We discussed safety in the workplace and driving regulations; he confirms he is not currently driving. He will contact us via the epilepsy specialist nurse if the frequency increases beyond weekly or if new features emerge such as prolonged confusion, falls, or injury. I will review him after the ambulatory study to plan next steps. 

Yours sincerely

Dr Patel
Harbour View Medical Centre

12 Quayside Road, Bristol, BS1 5AB

Dear Dr Patel

Michael Turner, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: H728391 NHS No. 9473826150
Flat 3, 28 Millpond Lane, Bristol, BS2 0DR

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today for ongoing follow-up of his seizures. I last saw him in March this year. Since then, his events have continued at a fairly regular cadence, occurring roughly once every seven to ten days. He feels that the frequency has not shifted since our previous review despite good adherence to medication.

Current medicines as reported today are: Carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily, Levetiracetam 1250 mg twice daily, Topiramate 100 mg twice daily, Sodium Valproate 500 mg twice daily, and Clobazam 10 mg at night. He notes manageable daytime sleepiness and occasional light-headedness on standing, without clear triggers for the events. He denies rashes but mentions intermittent tingling in his calves after longer walks. There have been no injuries, hospitalisations, or episodes requiring rescue therapy.

His partner has observed brief spells of reduced responsiveness on two occasions over the past month, each lasting under a minute, with rapid recovery and no confusion. He has also had one larger event about two weeks ago, witnessed at home, with whole-body stiffening and shaking described by his partner; recovery took approximately 30 minutes. These patterns are in keeping with his previous reports and remain at the same tempo. Sleep deprivation and missed meals seem to precede some attacks, though he is making efforts to maintain regular routines.

Neurological examination today is unremarkable. Weight and blood pressure are stable. We discussed safety, work routines, and strategies to minimise sleep disruption. He is keen to avoid medication changes until after further diagnostic clarification. I have arranged ambulatory EEG monitoring within the next month to better characterise the events and to guide any subsequent adjustments. Until we have the recording results, I have advised him to continue his current regimen as above and to keep a simple diary noting any aura-like symptoms, potential precipitants, and recovery details.

I will review him in clinic once the monitoring is completed. In the meantime, he has contact details for our epilepsy nurse specialist for practical advice and support.

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Centre

Neurosciences Division


From: Dr Emily Carter (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Sent: 02 October 2025 10:15
To: neuro.clinic@kch.nhs.uk
Cc: Dr Michael Hughes (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Priya Shah (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Subject: Clinic review and ongoing management

Hi Emily

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Type not specified in current records


Present Medication:

1. Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily
2. Clobazam 10 mg at night


Present Seizure Frequency:

Currently reporting monthly seizures, typically brief focal-onset episodes with rapid recovery as described by the family. Since commencing ketogenic diet therapy, the family notes a marked reduction in seizure frequency with only four brief seizures recorded in 2017 so far. This improvement has continued, and there have been no prolonged events or injuries this year.


Plan of Action:

At the last visit we made a minor adjustment by consolidating clobazam to night-time dosing while maintaining the lamotrigine dose. The patient and family report better sleep, improved alertness, and fewer breakthrough events, aligning with the pattern of monthly seizures only. No adverse effects have been noted from the ketogenic diet or current medications. We will:
- Continue lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily and clobazam 10 mg nocte unchanged.
- Maintain ketogenic diet therapy with ongoing dietetic support.
- Provide a rescue plan with buccal midazolam as previously prescribed for any seizure exceeding 5 minutes (not required to date).
- Monitor mood, sleep, and adherence; family to continue seizure diary and record any missed doses or intercurrent illness.
- Arrange routine bloods (U&E, LFTs, bicarbonate, lipid profile) and weight/BMI at the next nurse-led review in 3 months given the ongoing diet therapy.

The trajectory is clearly improving compared with previous years, with fewer and shorter events and stable cognition reported by school and parents. I will review again in 4 months, or sooner if the monthly seizures increase in duration, cluster, or result in injury.

With best wishes

Diagnoses/summary: History of recurrent unprovoked seizures of uncertain character and cause. Multiple routine EEGs previously nondiagnostic. No clear structural lesion identified on prior brain imaging per patient report.

Prior medication trials (per patient and records): Sodium valproate (sedation and tremor), carbamazepine (skin rash), levetiracetam (irritability), lamotrigine (insufficient benefit), clobazam PRN (helpful for clusters but daytime drowsiness). No history of topiramate, zonisamide, lacosamide, perampanel, or brivaracetam use.

Comorbidities: Mild hypertension (on amlodipine). No known cardiac murmur. No history of head injury or CNS infection. No family history of epilepsy recalled.

I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today. He is a newly retired secondary-school teacher living alone. He reports a predictable daily routine with early mornings, scheduled walks, and reduced social interaction since retirement. He keeps a seizure diary on paper and on his phone. He describes episodes that remain variably stereotyped. He notes that over the course of most calendar cycles he will have several events, sometimes in loose clusters, with longer quiet spells in between. He associates poorer sleep and missed meals with increased likelihood of events. He denies tongue biting or prolonged post-event confusion in every instance, though on occasion he experiences notable fatigue afterwards. There is no clear photic trigger, and he does not drive.

Current medication:
- Amlodipine 5 mg once daily
- Clobazam 10 mg at night PRN for clusters (used sparingly)
- Vitamin D 1000 IU once daily

Examination today was unremarkable. Weight stable. No focal neurological deficits. Blood pressure 138/82. He brought recent home BP readings which are broadly similar. Diary review suggests several events spread across most months, typically brief, with occasional back-to-back occurrences on successive days. No injuries reported.

Investigations and plans:
- Bloods today: FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, vitamin D level, thyroid function.
- Arrange MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) to update prior imaging from several years ago, as records provided were incomplete.
- Discussed treatment options, including introducing a different anti-seizure medicine. He wishes to consider this after reviewing the MRI and bloods. component_inputs.note_text:
KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 09 April 2019

Dr A. Patel
Riverside Medical Practice

12 Riverbank Way
London SE1 5AB
Dear Dr A. Patel
Michael Turner, DOB: 14-03-1955, Hospital No: H937521 NHS No. 8421905630
Flat 3, 28 Willow Street, London, SE1 3JT 

Diagnoses/summary: History of recurrent unprovoked seizures of uncertain character and cause. Multiple routine EEGs previously nondiagnostic. No clear structural lesion identified on prior brain imaging per patient report.

Prior medication trials (per patient and records): Sodium valproate (sedation and tremor), carbamazepine (skin rash), levetiracetam (irritability), lamotrigine (insufficient benefit), clobazam PRN (helpful for clusters but daytime drowsiness). No history of topiramate, zonisamide, lacosamide, perampanel, or brivaracetam use.

Comorbidities: Mild hypertension (on amlodipine). No known cardiac murmur. No history of head injury or CNS infection. No family history of epilepsy recalled.

I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today. He is a newly retired secondary-school teacher living alone. He reports a predictable daily routine with early mornings, scheduled walks, and reduced social interaction since retirement. He keeps a seizure diary on paper and on his phone. He describes episodes that remain variably stereotyped. He notes that over the course of most calendar cycles he will have several events, sometimes in loose clusters, with longer quiet spells in between. He associates poorer sleep and missed meals with increased likelihood of events. He denies tongue biting or prolonged post-event confusion in every instance, though on occasion he experiences notable fatigue afterwards. There is no clear photic trigger, and he does not drive.

Current medication:
- Amlodipine 5 mg once daily
- Clobazam 10 mg at night PRN for clusters (used sparingly)
- Vitamin D 1000 IU once daily

Examination today was unremarkable. Weight stable. No focal neurological deficits. Blood pressure 138/82. He brought recent home BP readings which are broadly similar. Diary review suggests several events spread across most months, typically brief, with occasional back-to-back occurrences on successive days. No injuries reported.

Investigations and plans:
- Bloods today: FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, vitamin D level, thyroid function.
- Arrange MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) to update prior imaging from several years ago, as records provided were incomplete.
- Discussed treatment options, including introducing a different anti-seizure medicine. He wishes to consider this after reviewing the MRI and bloods. We also discussed safety at home given that he lives alone: kettle use seated, avoiding high ladders, and considering a wearable alert device. He has already placed pans on back hobs and keeps the bathroom door unlocked.
- Agreed to continue clobazam PRN for short clusters only and to maintain a detailed seizure diary noting sleep, meals, and stressors.
- Provided information on local peer support groups; he will explore options that fit his routine to mitigate social isolation.

Follow-up:
- Telephone review by epilepsy nurse in 6–8 weeks to check diary, adherence, and side effects if any changes occur.
- Face-to-face clinic review in 3–4 months or sooner if events increase in intensity, duration, or lead to injury.
- Emergency plan discussed: seek urgent help if an event lasts longer than 5 minutes or if there are repeated events without full recovery.

Thank you for your continued care and support with blood pressure monitoring and general health maintenance. Please let me know if there are any concerns in the interim.

Yours sincerely

Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr Fiona
Centre for Epilepsy
Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG

Dear Dr Fiona,

Susan Miller, DOB: 14-05-1986, Hospital No: P948572 NHS No. 7623549812
12 Baker Street, London, NW1 6XE

Reason for review: Worsening seizure control following recent viral illness

Medication: Lamotrigine dispersible, currently 25 mg twice daily

Lamotrigine blood level:
28 September 2025: 1.2 mg/L (reference 1.0–15.0 mg/L). Dose at sampling: 25 mg twice daily.

Clinical summary:
I conducted a telephone review with Susan Miller today following her report of a recent viral illness (fever, myalgia, and sore throat approximately four weeks ago) and a subsequent deterioration in her seizure control. She reports 7 to 9 focal onset seizures in three weeks, describing brief episodes of impaired awareness with lip-smacking and a sense of fear, typically lasting under one minute and followed by mild confusion. These events were witnessed on two occasions at home by a family member. She denies generalised convulsions, tongue biting, or incontinence. There are no consistent auras reported, and no clear nocturnal clustering.

Comparison to prior baseline:
Prior to the viral illness, she described several months of relative stability without clear events interfering with daily activities. The recent cluster represents a significant change from her usual pattern and indicates deterioration in control.

Adherence and tolerability:
She reports taking lamotrigine as prescribed, without missed doses. No rash, no diplopia, and no gastrointestinal side effects. She has been more fatigued since the illness and notes increased stress at work, though sleep has been largely preserved.

Examination/investigations:
No examination was performed during this telephone review. Home blood pressure readings have been normal. No new medications or over-the-counter remedies except short courses of paracetamol during the illness. No alcohol excess. Pregnancy not suspected. Lamotrigine level as above.

Plan discussed with the patient:
- Safety advice reinforced, including avoidance of high-risk activities during this period of worsening episodes. She will maintain a seizure diary and record timings, potential triggers, and recovery features.
- She agrees to provide an updated account from her witness where possible to clarify semiology and frequency.
- I will review her case with the consultant team promptly in light of the reported 7 to 9 focal onset seizures in three weeks following the viral illness and the observed deterioration.
- We will arrange a follow-up telephone review within two weeks, or sooner if events escalate, and consider further investigations as needed depending on consultant recommendations.

I will keep you informed of any changes after the multidisciplinary review. Please let me know if there are concerns from your side, especially if she presents to primary care with further clustering.

Yours sincerely,

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Fiona  
Centre for Epilepsy  
Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG  

Dear Dr Fiona,

Daniel Harper, DOB: 22-11-1991, Hospital No: H604219 NHS No. 9842157630  
Flat 3, 27 Russell Square, London, WC1B 5HP  

Epilepsy 

Surgical history: Left temporal lobectomy performed March 2024; reports functional recovery and improved seizure control since surgery.

Medication: Ongoing Levetiracetam 1g twice daily; Clobazam 10mg at night as needed for clusters (rarely required). No adverse effects reported. 

Levetiracetam Blood Level:

16th September 2025: 19 mg/L (reference range 12–46 mg/L). Dose 1g twice a day. 

Seizures: Patient reports a clear reduction in events post-surgery. Specifically, 5 or 7 epileptic spasms this year, all brief (under 10 seconds), with rapid recovery and no injuries. No clear triggers identified. Family corroborate fewer events and improved day-to-day confidence. No auras or prolonged post-ictal confusion described.

I reviewed Daniel Harper today in face-to-face clinic. Since the temporal lobectomy in March 2024, they describe steady improvement in frequency and severity of episodes, better sleep, and return to part-time work without difficulties. They have maintained excellent adherence to Levetiracetam and have not required rescue Clobazam in the past three months. We discussed ongoing monitoring and agreed to continue current therapy without change. Safety advice and seizure diary use were reinforced; patient continues to avoid known personal precipitants and has informed their employer of their care plan. 

Plan:
- Continue Levetiracetam 1g twice daily.
- Clobazam 10mg nocte PRN for clusters; no routine use required at present.
- Maintain seizure diary; repeat medication review in six months.
- Routine bloods and Levetiracetam level prior to next appointment.

Yours sincerely

King's College Hospital 

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 31 March 2024 

Dr Amelia Hart
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr Amelia Hart
Consultant Neurologist,  

Daniel Roberts, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: D762345 NHS No. 9988776655  
12 Brookside Close, London, SE15 4DN

Thank you for asking me to review this patient in clinic today. He attended alone; his partner, who usually provides collateral, was unable to come. He reports that the majority of his events are at night, and this aligns with what his partner has previously told him. He keeps a basic diary at the bedside and cross-checks with his partner the following day to clarify what was observed.

Over the past month he has recorded four focal sensory and five focal non-motors in last month, almost all occurring between 01:00 and 05:00, giving a total of nine events per month. He describes the sensory episodes as brief internal tingling with a rising abdominal sensation, preserved awareness, and no subsequent confusion. The non-motor episodes are described as sudden behavioural arrest noticed on waking (waking partially with awareness of being "stuck"), with subsequent fatigue but no tongue biting or incontinence. He denies clear daytime triggers, though he notes that poor sleep and late meals appear to correlate with clusters.

There is no new head injury, febrile illness, or medication change reported. He remains on Brivaracetam 100 mg twice daily and Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily, taken reliably per his account. He has not driven for over a year and is aware of DVLA guidance. Neurological examination today was unremarkable, and there were no focal deficits. Mood was stable; he denies hallucinations or delusional ideas. Cognitive screening was within expected limits for age and education.

Given that the events are predominantly nocturnal and the partner was not present today, objective corroboration remains limited. I have advised continuation of the seizure diary and suggested using his smartphone to record overnight audio where feasible. I will arrange an ambulatory EEG with overnight capture to better characterise the events, and I have requested prior MRI images from his local radiology archive for review. We discussed general measures around sleep hygiene and medication adherence. He is agreeable to proceed with the investigations and a follow-up in three months or sooner if there is an escalation in frequency or any injury.

Yours sincerely

Clinic Date: 05 April 2023 

Dr A. Patel
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital

Dear Dr A. Patel
Consultant Neurologist,  

Daniel Harris, DOB: 14-03-1982, Hospital No: KCH742915 NHS No. 9065183274  
78 Brookfield Road, London, SE15 2LP

Thank you for asking me to review your patient. He attended with his partner and provided a clear diary of recent events. Unfortunately, there is evidence of clinical deterioration over the past month. He reports increased day-to-day difficulty with concentration, intermittent word-finding pauses, and escalating fatigue and irritability that he attributes to his current polytherapy. Adverse effects are becoming bothersome (notably daytime somnolence, unsteadiness on rapid head turns, and blunted mood), yet seizure control remains suboptimal. Over the last week he recorded five focal cognitive and six focal non-motors in last week, occurring at variable times without an obvious precipitant. Several of these were clustered over two consecutive mornings, with prolonged post-event disorientation on one occasion. His partner also notes brief nocturnal arousals with confusion, though no clear witnessed generalised convulsions.

He remains adherent to medication and has not missed doses; he denies alcohol or illicit substance use. Sleep has been fragmented, in part due to early-morning awakenings. He is using a smartphone seizure diary, and we reviewed consistent timestamped entries. There has been no recent intercurrent illness. He has not driven and understands the DVLA guidance as previously discussed.

Examination today was non-focal. Gait was steady on slow turns but he felt light-headed on tandem stepping. No papilloedema. Cardiovascular and systemic review unremarkable. Mood was subdued but there was no thought disorder or psychotic features. 

Investigations to date include a prior routine EEG (last year) that was non-diagnostic and a brain MRI (18 months ago) reported as structurally unremarkable. Given the current pattern and the worsening frequency and impact, I am concerned that, despite polytherapy, control is not adequate and tolerability is poor. We discussed the need to clarify the electroclinical pattern and to consider rationalisation of treatment if safe to do so. He is agreeable to expedited prolonged video-EEG monitoring as an inpatient, and I will request this urgently. I will also arrange updated bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, vitamin D, thyroid function) and drug levels where available to check for toxicity or interactions contributing to the adverse effects.

We reviewed general measures: regular sleep schedule, hydration, and avoidance of missed meals. He and his partner are aware of seizure first aid and have a plan to escalate if events become longer or different in character. I provided contact details for our epilepsy nurse specialist for interim support while we await telemetry.

King's College Hospital 

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 05 April 2023 

Dr A. Patel
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr A. Patel
Consultant Neurologist,  

Daniel Harris, DOB: 14-03-1982, Hospital No: KCH742915 NHS No. 9065183274  
78 Brookfield Road, London, SE15 2LP

Thank you for asking me to review your patient. He attended with his partner and provided a clear diary of recent events. Unfortunately, there is evidence of clinical deterioration over the past month. He reports increased day-to-day difficulty with concentration, intermittent word-finding pauses, and escalating fatigue and irritability that he attributes to his current polytherapy. Adverse effects are becoming bothersome (notably daytime somnolence, unsteadiness on rapid head turns, and blunted mood), yet seizure control remains suboptimal. Over the last week he recorded five focal cognitive and six focal non-motors in last week, occurring at variable times without an obvious precipitant. Several of these were clustered over two consecutive mornings, with prolonged post-event disorientation on one occasion. His partner also notes brief nocturnal arousals with confusion, though no clear witnessed generalised convulsions.

He remains adherent to medication and has not missed doses; he denies alcohol or illicit substance use. Sleep has been fragmented, in part due to early-morning awakenings. He is using a smartphone seizure diary, and we reviewed consistent timestamped entries. There has been no recent intercurrent illness. He has not driven and understands the DVLA guidance as previously discussed.

Examination today was non-focal. Gait was steady on slow turns but he felt light-headed on tandem stepping. No papilloedema. Cardiovascular and systemic review unremarkable. Mood was subdued but there was no thought disorder or psychotic features. 

Investigations to date include a prior routine EEG (last year) that was non-diagnostic and a brain MRI (18 months ago) reported as structurally unremarkable. Given the current pattern and the worsening frequency and impact, I am concerned that, despite polytherapy, control is not adequate and tolerability is poor. We discussed the need to clarify the electroclinical pattern and to consider rationalisation of treatment if safe to do so. He is agreeable to expedited prolonged video-EEG monitoring as an inpatient, and I will request this urgently. I will also arrange updated bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, vitamin D, thyroid function) and drug levels where available to check for toxicity or interactions contributing to the adverse effects.

We reviewed general measures: regular sleep schedule, hydration, and avoidance of missed meals. He and his partner are aware of seizure first aid and have a plan to escalate if events become longer or different in character. I provided contact details for our epilepsy nurse specialist for interim support while we await telemetry. 

I will update you once monitoring is completed and results are available. In the meantime, I have not altered his current regimen today due to the risk of further destabilisation, but the trajectory is concerning, and I anticipate we may need to rationalise therapy soon depending on monitoring findings and tolerability.

Yours sincerely

Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Amelia Khan  
Centre for Epilepsy  
Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG  

Dear Dr Amelia Khan,                                                                                                         

Katie Robinson, DOB: 22-11-1993, Hospital No: H627391 NHS No. 9837456210  
Flat 5, 28 Wenlock Road, London, N1 7TA  

Generalised Epilepsy 

Medication: Ongoing Levetiracetam since March 2024  

Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily (patient-reported adherence without missed doses)  

Levetiracetam Blood Level:  

15 September 2025: 18 mg/L (laboratory reference 12–46 mg/L). Dose 750 mg twice daily.  

Seizures: The patient reports five focal onset seizures and six focal non-motors in last month. These events were most commonly precipitated during exposure to flicker or bright light, including sun flicker through trees while travelling by bus, and while using a large-screen television in the evening. There were no generalised tonic–clonic seizures reported in the same interval. The focal onset episodes were brief with impaired awareness and lip-smacking observed by family; the focal non-motor events were described as sudden arrest of activity with internal déjà vu sensation and pallor, typically lasting under one minute and followed by mild fatigue. No auras of visual zig-zags or headache were noted. 

History since last review: Patient has generalised epilepsy with photosensitivity noted during prior EEG (photoparoxysmal response at 15–20 Hz), and she continues to avoid strobe environments where possible. She has started a new job with variable lighting conditions and reports that the onset of the recent cluster coincided with prolonged screen time and commuting on bright days. Sleep has been fair (6–7 hours/night). No alcohol intake. No recent intercurrent illness. 

Risk/Safety: She is aware of seizure first aid and avoids swimming alone. No driving currently; she understands DVLA guidance and will maintain a seizure diary. 

Plan: Patient will maintain a detailed seizure and trigger log, including light exposure details. She will utilise blue-light reduction and regular rest breaks with screens as tolerated. I have arranged a follow-up EEG with intermittent photic stimulation to reassess photosensitivity under current medication. We discussed general measures to minimise flicker exposure in daily settings. She is satisfied with the plan and will contact the clinic earlier if events change in pattern or severity. 

Yours sincerely

With best wishes

Subject: Worsening events and medication adjustment

Hi Priya

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Diagnosis remains under ongoing evaluation; classification not yet determined.

Present Medication:

1. Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily
2. Topiramate 50 mg twice daily

Present Seizure Frequency:

two drop attacks and three petit mal in last month

Clinical Update and Concern:

Over the past six weeks the patient reports clear deterioration. Specifically, aura characteristics have changed from a brief metallic taste to a new pattern of sudden heat flush, muffled hearing, and a rapid sense of detachment lasting 5–10 seconds, now evolving more quickly into impaired awareness. There is no consistent precipitant identified. Witness accounts describe abrupt loss of tone with forward slump on two occasions, resulting in minor facial bruising, and three brief staring spells with lip-smacking and unresponsiveness, each under one minute, followed by fatigue and headache. No recent intercurrent illness, alcohol, or sleep deprivation reported.

Examination today is non-focal. Bloods last month (U&Es, LFTs, FBC) were within reference ranges. Lamotrigine and topiramate levels are not routinely measured here but adherence appears good by patient report and pharmacy refill history. A prior MRI (18 months ago) was unremarkable. Given the evolving auras and more rapid progression to events, this represents a deterioration from the previous stable period.

Plan of Action:

1) Safety: Advised strict adherence to seizure precautions including avoidance of heights, swimming unsupervised, and cooking with open flames. Reinforced DVLA guidance regarding events with impaired awareness or drop attacks; the patient understands not to drive.

2) Medication: Increase topiramate from 50 mg twice daily to 50 mg in the morning and 75 mg at night for one week, then 75 mg twice daily thereafter if tolerated. Maintain lamotrigine at the current dose for now.

3) Rescue strategy: Provided written advice for carers regarding recovery position and timing of events; no home rescue medication initiated at this stage as events remain brief without convulsive generalisation.

4) Investigations: Arrange urgent outpatient video-EEG with hyperventilation and photic stimulation, and repeat MRI brain with epilepsy protocol given the change in semiology. We will also screen for metabolic precipitants (glucose, magnesium) and repeat routine bloods.

Epilepsy Centre

Neurosciences Division


From: Dr Priya Shah (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Sent: 07 September 2021 10:15
To: neuro.epilepsy@nhs.net
Cc: Dr Michael Green (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Emily Clarke (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Subject: Worsening events and medication adjustment

Hi Priya

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Diagnosis remains under ongoing evaluation; classification not yet determined.

Present Medication:

1. Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily
2. Topiramate 50 mg twice daily

Present Seizure Frequency:

two drop attacks and three petit mal in last month

Clinical Update and Concern:

Over the past six weeks the patient reports clear deterioration. Specifically, aura characteristics have changed from a brief metallic taste to a new pattern of sudden heat flush, muffled hearing, and a rapid sense of detachment lasting 5–10 seconds, now evolving more quickly into impaired awareness. There is no consistent precipitant identified. Witness accounts describe abrupt loss of tone with forward slump on two occasions, resulting in minor facial bruising, and three brief staring spells with lip-smacking and unresponsiveness, each under one minute, followed by fatigue and headache. No recent intercurrent illness, alcohol, or sleep deprivation reported.

Examination today is non-focal. Bloods last month (U&Es, LFTs, FBC) were within reference ranges. Lamotrigine and topiramate levels are not routinely measured here but adherence appears good by patient report and pharmacy refill history. A prior MRI (18 months ago) was unremarkable. Given the evolving auras and more rapid progression to events, this represents a deterioration from the previous stable period.

Plan of Action:

1) Safety: Advised strict adherence to seizure precautions including avoidance of heights, swimming unsupervised, and cooking with open flames. Reinforced DVLA guidance regarding events with impaired awareness or drop attacks; the patient understands not to drive.

2) Medication: Increase topiramate from 50 mg twice daily to 50 mg in the morning and 75 mg at night for one week, then 75 mg twice daily thereafter if tolerated. Maintain lamotrigine at the current dose for now.

3) Rescue strategy: Provided written advice for carers regarding recovery position and timing of events; no home rescue medication initiated at this stage as events remain brief without convulsive generalisation.

4) Investigations: Arrange urgent outpatient video-EEG with hyperventilation and photic stimulation, and repeat MRI brain with epilepsy protocol given the change in semiology. We will also screen for metabolic precipitants (glucose, magnesium) and repeat routine bloods.

5) Follow-up: I have brought the review forward to 6 weeks. If events continue or worsen despite the above adjustment, we will discuss alternative therapy at that visit.

Please let me know if you have any concerns in the interim.

With best wishes

- Follow-up: telephone review in 8 weeks timed to his onshore period, or sooner if he experiences any convulsive seizures, clusters, or injuries.

She reports two drop attacks and nine absence seizures in the past six months. These were not clustered and there were no known triggers identified. She has not engaged with talking therapies previously but is open to self-referral to IAPT for support with anxiety/low mood. She prefers to avoid any changes to her current anti-seizure medicines at present, given tolerability and the relatively low frequency of events over the half-year period.

Epilepsy Centre 

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 27 March 2014 

Dr Patel  
St George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust  
Neurology Outpatients, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT  

Dear Dr Patel,  

Emily Harper, DOB: 14-02-1990, Hospital No: H482917 NHS No. 9081764523  
12 Willow Close, London, SW12 8JR  

Diagnoses: 

Recurrent seizures. 

Thank you for referring Emily Harper back to clinic. She attended today with her partner. She described fluctuating mood over the past year, with periods of anxiety and low mood particularly around times of uncertainty at work. She has not had any recent medication changes. She reports two drop attacks and nine absence seizures in the past six months. These were not clustered and there were no known triggers identified. No injuries were sustained, though she did report one near-fall at home and has since taken practical precautions (e.g. using handrails on stairs). 

She is currently taking lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 1 g twice daily, which she has tolerated without rash, behavioural change, or dose-limiting adverse effects. Adherence is reported as good; she uses a phone reminder and a weekly pill organiser. Rescue medication is not prescribed, and there have been no attendances to A&E. She denies prolonged events, tongue biting, or incontinence. There is no recent sleep deprivation, alcohol misuse, or intercurrent illness reported. 

Examination in clinic was unremarkable with normal cardiorespiratory observations and no focal neurological deficit. No nystagmus or ataxia observed. 

We discussed the interaction between mood/anxiety and seizure threshold. She feels the worry about having another event increases her day-to-day anxiety, particularly on public transport. She has not engaged with talking therapies previously but is open to self-referral to IAPT for support with anxiety/low mood. She prefers to avoid any changes to her current anti-seizure medicines at present, given tolerability and the relatively low frequency of events over the half-year period. 

Plan: 
- No changes to anti-seizure medication today at her request; continue lamotrigine and levetiracetam at current doses.  
- Provide seizure diary and safety guidance; reinforce adherence and sleep hygiene.  
- Signpost to local IAPT service for anxiety/low mood; patient to self-refer.  
- Routine bloods arranged today (U&Es, LFTs, FBC) to monitor general health; no dose-related concerns identified clinically.  
- DVLA guidance reviewed; patient confirms she is not currently driving and understands requirements to inform DVLA if applicable.  
- Follow-up in six months, or sooner if the pattern changes (increase in frequency, injuries, or prolonged events). 

Please do not hesitate to contact me if further information is required. 

Yours sincerely

Clinic Date: 30 August 2015 

Dr Wang
Saffron Park Hospital

Saffron Park, London, E14 7JL
Dear Dr Wang
John Doe, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: P546484 NHS No. 5484656746
Flat 15 Roundwood Road, London, E14 7JL 

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. He remains under follow‑up for recurrent seizures. Since I last corresponded, he has continued to keep a detailed diary and has synchronised entries from a menstrual tracking app used by his partner to help contextualise potential catamenial influences noted in his own calendar. Over the past four months he reports six drop attacks and two epileptic spasms in the past four months. These events have tended to cluster around predicted luteal–menses windows based on the shared app entries and his own symptom notes (fatigue, irritability, and premonitory light‑headedness). He denies any prolonged convulsive episodes, tongue‑bite, or injury beyond minor bruising from the drop attacks.

Current treatment consists of Levetiracetam 1 g b.d. and Lamotrigine 150 mg b.d., both reportedly well tolerated. He describes intermittent morning lethargy and word‑finding difficulty on busy workdays, but no rash, mood lability beyond baseline, or gastrointestinal upset. Adherence is good; he uses phone reminders and a weekly pill organiser. There are no new intercurrent illnesses, he drinks minimal alcohol, and sleeps 6–7 hours nightly, though he notes sleep fragmentation in the days preceding the clusters.

Neurological examination today was unremarkable. There are no new focal neurological symptoms. Routine bloods from last month (FBC, U&E, LFTs) were within normal limits per GP records. He has arranged to continue cross‑referencing his seizure diary with the menstrual tracking app entries to clarify the temporal pattern over the next cycle set. We discussed the observational nature of this approach and he is agreeable to sharing anonymised app screenshots at the next review to corroborate timing.

At present I have not altered his medication. I have asked him to maintain strict seizure and trigger documentation, including sleep duration, stressors, and the app‑referenced cycle dates, to help determine whether the apparent catamenial pattern is consistent. If the pattern persists, we can consider options at review. I will also request an updated EEG and arrange a follow‑up in three months, sooner if events escalate or injuries occur.

Yours sincerely

St Mary's Hospital 

Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Ahmed  
St Mary's Hospital  
Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY  

Dear Dr Ahmed,  

Sophie Williams, DOB: 12-11-1993, Hospital No: H458210 NHS No. 5938472016  
24 Brookside Avenue, London, W10 5LP 

Medication: 

Levetiracetam 1000 mg/1000 mg. Lamotrigine previously trialled up to 100 mg bd but stopped due to rash; topiramate discontinued after cognitive slowing. 

Since her last review she has been using a smartwatch with fall-detection enabled; the device has generated time-stamped alerts that align with events witnessed by her partner and entries in her symptom diary. Over the past two months she reports six drop attacks and two absence seizures in the past two months, typically occurring in the late afternoon. The smartwatch recorded three fall alerts corresponding to two witnessed collapses at home and one in the supermarket; the latter resulted in minor bruising to the right hip without head injury. The two absence episodes were brief (under 20 seconds) with immediate recovery, noted during conversations and corroborated by gaps in her activity log.

She denies clear triggers, though she notes poor sleep in the week preceding two of the drop attacks and higher work-related stress. No alcohol excess. She remains fully adherent to levetiracetam and uses a weekly pill organiser. No recent infections. Menses regular; she has not noted a cyclical pattern. Family have been educated on first aid, and she has enabled the smartwatch feature that texts her partner if a fall is detected.

Neurological examination today is normal. Weight stable. No adverse effects from levetiracetam apart from mild irritability, which she considers manageable. I have advised maintaining her current regimen for now while we clarify the pattern of events. I have also asked her to continue synchronising smartwatch alerts with her diary and to bring screenshots of the alert timeline to the next visit. We discussed safety: avoiding baths unsupervised, taking showers with the door unlocked, and using the handset’s emergency SOS if she feels premonitory symptoms. She is not currently driving and understands to inform DVLA should events continue; we reviewed standard guidance.

Plan: 
- Continue levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. 
- Arrange EEG and MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) to aid further characterisation. 
- Bloods: FBC, U&Es, LFTs, vitamin D. 
- Provide written seizure first-aid advice and signpost to local support group. 
- Review in three months, sooner if drop attacks increase or injuries occur. 

We will see her back in three months. 

Yours sincerely

Subject: Worsening seizure control post-partum

Dear Emma,

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

The patient has generalised epilepsy.

Current Concerns and Context:

Since delivering her baby recently, she reports notable low mood and significant fatigue. She perceives that her seizure control has deteriorated in this post-partum period, and her partner corroborates increased episodes of brief behavioural arrest and sudden drops without warning. Sleep is fragmented due to night feeds, and she feels more anxious about caring for the newborn when alone.

Present Medication:

1. Tegretol Retard 600 mg twice daily
2. Keppra 500 mg twice daily

Present Seizure Frequency:

She reports one drop attacks and seven absence seizures in the past two months. These have clustered around periods of marked sleep deprivation.

Assessment:

The temporal relationship with the post-partum period, compounded by low mood and fatigue, is consistent with her perceived deterioration. There are no intercurrent illnesses or missed doses reported. No clear provoking factors beyond sleep disruption have been identified.

Plan of Action:

- Safety and support: We have discussed practical safety measures for drop attacks, including avoiding carrying the baby on stairs and using seated changing where possible. She will keep a seizure diary noting sleep, mood, and timing of episodes.
- Monitoring: We will arrange a follow-up in eight weeks to review seizure burden, mood, and sleep patterns, and to reassess management once the post-partum routine stabilises.
- Communication: She understands to contact the service promptly if drop attacks increase or injuries occur.

I will keep you updated following her next review.

Dear Dr Ahmed
Michael Carter, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: NHS847201 NHS No. 7483926159
22B Millbank Court, London, SW1P 3SY 

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. He has Combined Generalised and Focal Epilepsy Type, with a history indicating both generalised and focal epilepsy. Since his last review, his condition has been deteriorating. He reports recent events associated with falls and minor injuries, including a bruised shoulder and abrasions to the knees following unwitnessed collapses at home and while commuting. Prior to this deterioration, his seizure frequency was three clusters this month; each ≈four absences in the morning, which he described as brief staring spells with impaired awareness and rapid recovery.

Over the past two months he has experienced one drop attacks and seven convulsions in the past two months. The convulsions have been predominantly generalised tonic–clonic events occurring without clear warning, twice from sleep, with post-ictal confusion lasting up to an hour. In addition, he describes focal onset events with a rising epigastric sensation, brief speech arrest and right-hand automatisms, occurring several times per week, some evolving into generalised convulsions. His partner has noted eyelid fluttering and brief behavioural arrest consistent with generalised absence phenomena on several mornings. He denies tongue-biting but reports occasional urinary incontinence after the longer convulsions.

Medication at present: Lamotrigine 200 mg b.d., Levetiracetam 1 g b.d., and Lacosamide 150 mg b.d. He is adherent by report, using a pill organiser and smartphone reminders. He notes increased tiredness and occasional light-headedness but no rash or mood change. There is no reported alcohol excess; sleep has been fragmented due to nocturnal events. He remains employed but has missed shifts due to recovery days after convulsions. He does not drive.

Neurological examination today was non-focal. Cardiovascular observations were stable. There is mild tenderness over the right deltoid consistent with recent soft-tissue injury. We reviewed seizure first aid, injury precautions, and safety around bathing and heights. Given the clear increase in event burden and the emergence of drop attacks with injury, I have arranged an expedited video-EEG telemetry admission and an updated MRI brain with epilepsy protocol. I have also requested serum antiepileptic drug levels (where applicable), U&E, LFT, FBC, and vitamin D. We discussed interim strategies including ensuring adequate sleep, stress management, and consistent medication timing. 

I will revisit his regimen once we have the telemetry and imaging data, as the mixed semiologies support his known diagnosis of combined generalised and focal epilepsy, and treatment adjustment may be needed. I have provided him with an emergency care plan and advised his employer regarding phased duties to reduce risk pending further evaluation.

Yours sincerely

St Mary's Hospital

Institute of Neurology

Clinic Date: 12 September 2025

Dr Shah
St Mary's Hospital
Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY

Dear Dr Shah,

Re: Amelia Thompson, DOB: 22-11-1990, Hospital No: H938420, NHS No. 6842951730
14 Brookside Avenue, London, W2 5JP

Diagnosis and history:
Amelia Thompson is followed in our service for focal epilepsy. She reports that over the past three months she has experienced two drop attacks and five tonic-clonic in the past three months. This frequency reflects her typical pattern over the preceding quarters, and remains unchanged following the most recent treatment adjustments.

Current medication:
• Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily.
• Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily.
She reports good adherence without notable adverse effects beyond occasional irritability and mild insomnia, which she attributes to stress at work. No rashes, no cognitive complaints, and no new neurological symptoms were reported.

Assessment:
Her description of brief focal aware episodes (epigastric rising sensation and déjà vu) occasionally progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures is in keeping with focal epilepsy, likely temporal lobe onset. Despite optimised adherence, the overall seizure burden has not changed; specifically, she has had two drop attacks and five tonic-clonic in the past three months. There is no clear diurnal pattern. She denies alcohol excess and recreational drug use. Sleep is variable due to shift work, which may be a contributory factor.

Plan:
• Continue current antiseizure medications at the present doses, as there has been no deterioration but also no improvement in the count of two drop attacks and five tonic-clonic in the past three months.
• Arrange MRI brain with epilepsy protocol (3T) and repeat EEG with sleep deprivation to refine localisation.
• Provide written advice on sleep hygiene and seizure triggers; patient will review feasibility of reducing night shifts with her employer.
• Safety counselled regarding drop attacks and convulsive seizures at home and in public; discussed SUDEP awareness and first-aid guidance with her and her partner.
• Driving: she has already informed the DVLA and is not driving.

Follow-up:
We will review her in clinic in four months or sooner if events escalate, injuries occur, or medication side effects emerge.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Priya Shah

Dear Dr Priya Shah
Consultant Neurologist,  

Daniel Carter, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: KCH783221 NHS No. 9432175609  
12 Brookfield Road, London, SE15 3HT

Thank you for asking me to review your patient. He is known to have type 2 diabetes managed in primary care, but today’s consultation focused on his seizures. He attended with his partner, who keeps a diary of events. According to their records, he has had four absence seizures and one myoclonic this month. These have been brief, typically seconds for the absences with preserved posture, and a single morning myoclonic jerk that caused him to drop a cup. There has been no reported loss of continence, tongue biting, or prolonged post-event confusion. He has noticed that poor sleep and late nights seem to precede some of the absences. 

He reports taking his current anti-seizure medication regularly, without missed doses, and denies alcohol or recreational drug use. There is no clear pattern to the timing of the absences other than occasional clustering on workdays when he skips breakfast. He has not driven and is aware of DVLA regulations as previously advised by his GP. He recalls a remote head injury in adolescence without hospitalisation; no family history of seizures was reported. 

Neurological examination today was unremarkable. Cardiovascular and general examination were stable. Capillary glucose in clinic was within his usual range per his home log, and he continues diabetes management through his GP. 

I have requested updated routine EEG and will arrange an outpatient MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) given the ongoing events. I have also asked him to continue the seizure diary and to record any potential triggers, especially sleep deprivation, missed meals, or intercurrent illness. We discussed basic safety measures at home and at work, and he agreed to share a brief summary with his line manager. 

I will review him after the investigations to reassess management. In the meantime, he will maintain current therapy and contact us earlier if the frequency worsens, if there are prolonged episodes, or if there is any injury. 

Thank you for your referral and for continuing his diabetes care in primary care. Please let me know if there are concerns in the interim. 

Yours sincerely

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE

Clinic Date: 08 October 2019

Dr Patel
Riverside Health Centre

1 Wharf Lane, Southwark, London SE1 2AB
Dear Dr Patel
Wendy Brown, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: K482715 NHS No. 6592841037
Flat 7 Brookside Avenue, Newcastle-under-Lyme, ST5 2QD

Diagnoses/summary: Drug-resistant focal epilepsy, likely temporal lobe onset. Prior prolonged EEG/telemetry on multiple occasions. MRI (2006) reported no clear epileptogenic lesion. Reported cardiac murmur historically; echocardiogram in 2008 essentially normal.

Occupational context: Works in a cold-chain warehouse (sustained low temperatures). Gloves and chilled environment can slow fine-motor handling of rescue devices, especially during post-ictal periods.

Current presentation: I reviewed Wendy Brown in clinic today; she attended alone. She describes ongoing focal aware and focal impaired-awareness episodes with auras of rising epigastric discomfort and transient speech arrest, sometimes with lip smacking. She has had occasional tonic-clonic over last year, typically evolving from focal onset and tending to cluster during periods of sleep deprivation or shift changes at work. Post-ictal confusion lasts 15–30 minutes. No new head injuries reported. She notes intermittent paraesthesia in fingers when working in the freezer bays and says donning thick gloves can delay access to her rescue medication pouch. She also reports increased daytime fatigue and occasional mild headaches. Appetite stable; weight unchanged. No current pregnancy plans.

Medication history:
- Previous: Levetiracetam (reduced intensity but caused irritability and fatigue), Clobazam (regular and PRN trials), Gabapentin, Carbamazepine, Phenobarbitone, Phenytoin, Valproate, Vigabatrin, Lacosamide (discontinued for dizziness), and a trial of Lamotrigine in the past with partial response.
- Not taken to date: Pregabalin, Zonisamide, Tiagabine, Acetazolamide, Primidone, Perampanel, Retigabine, Rufinamide.

Current medication:
- Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily.
- Metoclopramide as needed for nausea.
- Folic acid 5 mg daily and a general multivitamin.

Additional notes: Prior discussions regarding neuromodulation (VNS) documented. The patient remains open to device-based therapy but is concerned about any downtime from work scheduling. She carries a rescue benzodiazepine; however, she reports that in sub-zero bays the zip on the pouch can stick and gloves slow administration, leading to delay of a few minutes. She is exploring a pouch with a larger pull tab and a front-zip uniform pocket. She has no history of glaucoma; vision checks up to date. Mood stable; no recent depression or psychosis. Sleep is fragmented due to rotating shifts. Family history notable for a sibling with kidney stones, making her slightly wary of carbonic anhydrase inhibitor–related risks.

Examination today: Alert and oriented. Speech fluent, no dysarthria. Cranial nerves intact. No focal motor deficits. Coordination and gait normal. Cardiovascular exam unremarkable. No cutaneous stigmata. Observed mild hand chilliness post-commute from work site.

Investigations: Historic MRI (2006) with no definite epileptogenic lesion. Prior EEGs/telemetries consistent with temporal lobe focal onset. No new imaging since last review; bloods last month within reference, including bicarbonate.

Plan:
- We discussed medication options including Zonisamide and Topiramate. Given her sibling’s renal stone history and her concern about cold-related dehydration in the warehouse, we reviewed hydration, renal stone risk, cognition/word-finding issues, and weight change. She prefers a cautious trial of Topiramate with close monitoring. I issued a starter prescription for 25 mg nightly. A nurse will telephone at 4–6 week intervals to assess tolerability and consider gradual titration if beneficial. Side-effects explained today (paresthesia, word-finding difficulty, mood change, weight loss, rare glaucoma) and the importance of adequate fluid intake even in cold settings was emphasised.
- Safety and access: We discussed practical adaptations for the cold-chain environment, including a larger zip pull and outer pocket placement of rescue medication. She will trial a breakaway lanyard clip and a thermal pouch to reduce stiffness of packaging. Workplace first-aider informed (with her consent) of typical focal impaired-awareness signs and that the occasional tonic-clonic over last year have followed focal onset. She requested a concise seizure action plan card; we provided this today, including when to call 999.
- Sleep and shifts: Advised consistent sleep windows where rota permits; she will request fewer rapid turnarounds between night and early shifts. She will track seizures relative to shift pattern in a diary.
- Follow-up: Routine review in 3 months, sooner if increased seizure frequency, adverse effects, or any visual symptoms (â€ warning given regarding acute eye pain/redness). Consider updated MRI with epilepsy protocol if limited response to optimisation. VNS can be revisited once medication pathway clarified.

Thank you for continuing her prescriptions if tolerated and for monitoring interim progress. Please let me know if there are any concerns. I remain happy to see Wendy Brown earlier as needed.

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Centre

Neurosciences Division


From: Dr Priya Shah (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Sent: 27 June 2019 11:20
To: epilepsy.clinic@nhs.net
Cc: Dr Michael Turner (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Helen Brooks (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Subject: Treatment review and guidance

Hi Priya

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Generalised epilepsy


Present Medication:

1. Sodium Valproate 300 mg in the morning and 500 mg at night
2. Lamotrigine 50 mg twice daily


Present Seizure Frequency:

Patient reports frequent petit mal recently, particularly on waking and during periods of prolonged screen use at work. No generalised tonic–clonic seizures for over a year.


Plan of Action:

The patient describes increasing brief absence episodes over the past six weeks, with no clear illness, sleep deprivation, or missed doses identified. They feel work-related visual strain and stress may be contributory. Given the pattern in generalised epilepsy, I recommend a cautious optimisation of lamotrigine while maintaining sodium valproate.

Please adjust Lamotrigine as follows: increase to 75 mg twice daily for two weeks, then to 100 mg twice daily thereafter, provided no rash or adverse effects occur. Continue Sodium Valproate at the current dose. If sedation or tremor emerge, please let me know, as we may need to fine-tune the evening valproate dose.

I have advised the patient on regular sleep, breaks from screen exposure (20–20–20 rule), and to keep a seizure diary documenting time of day, precipitating factors, and functional impact. They will also arrange an optometry review to reduce visual strain at work.

I will review them in clinic in three months. If the frequent petit mal recently persist despite the above, we will consider substituting valproate with ethosuximide or adjusting therapy toward levetiracetam, balancing efficacy and tolerability.

With best wishes

Department of Neurology

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr Amelia Grant
South Thames Neurology Centre
2nd Floor, Riverside Wing, St Martin’s Hospital, London SE11 3PA

Dear Dr Amelia Grant,

Michael Turner, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: H392771 NHS No. 9472158036
Flat 5, 28 Willow Street, London, EC2A 4BH

Diagnoses:

Recurrent unprovoked seizures (classification not established)

Current medication:

Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily
Rescue: Buccal midazolam 10 mg as needed for prolonged events

Plan:

- Increase Levetiracetam to 750 mg twice daily
- Continue safety and lifestyle measures; maintain seizure diary app use
- MRI brain with epilepsy protocol and routine EEG
- Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFTs, Vitamin D
- DVLA guidance reinforced; no driving
- Follow-up in 8–10 weeks or sooner if events escalate

I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today. He shared detailed entries from his seizure diary app, including time-stamped logs, associated symptoms, and potential triggers. Over the last fortnight, he has logged about 3 or 5 seizures in the last two weeks, with events typically occurring in the early morning shortly after waking. The diary entries describe brief loss of awareness with bilateral limb stiffening and jerking lasting 60–90 seconds, followed by confusion and headache for up to 30 minutes. No clear precipitant is identified, although he noted reduced sleep and higher work-related stress preceding two of the events.

There is no tongue biting or urinary incontinence reported in recent episodes. He has sustained minor bruising from one fall without head injury. No focal neurological symptoms between events. He denies alcohol or recreational drug use. Family history is non-contributory. He commenced Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily three months ago with good tolerability (mild irritability noted in the diary during the first two weeks which has since settled). Despite adherence, the recent increase in frequency captured on the app suggests suboptimal control.

Examination today was unremarkable with normal cardiorespiratory and neurological findings. Baseline blood tests from June were within normal limits. To progress evaluation, I have arranged an MRI brain with an epilepsy protocol and a routine EEG to look for supportive features, and I have asked him to continue using the diary app and to upload videos if safe for bystanders to capture. We discussed safety: supervised bathing, avoiding heights/open water, and using a microwave rather than open hob when alone. DVLA regulations were reviewed; he understands he must not drive and has agreed to notify the DVLA if he has not already done so.

Given the recent pattern recorded in the app, I have recommended increasing Levetiracetam to 750 mg twice daily. He has a supply and understands a simple up-titration over three days. Buccal midazolam remains for rescue in prolonged events. I have provided our urgent advice line details should the frequency increase further or if he experiences any new features such as prolonged clusters, injuries, or atypical focal symptoms.

I will review him in 8–10 weeks with the imaging and EEG results and will reassess treatment options based on response and investigations.

With best wishes,

Yours sincerely,
