component_inputs.note_text:
St Mary's Hospital 

Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 02 March 2017 

Dr Patel  
St Mary's Hospital  
Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY  

Dear Dr Patel,  

Emily Carter, DOB: 17-08-1989, Hospital No: C672154 NHS No. 4728395612  
78 Willow Lane, London, W9 3HT 

Medication: 

Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. Previously stable on this dose for several months.

I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today. She reports a deterioration in seizure control over the past 6 weeks coinciding with a change in her workplace environment, where she is now regularly exposed to strong and intermittently flickering lights in an open-plan office with large display screens. She describes 6 to 7 myoclonic per week, predominantly occurring on workdays and chiefly in the late morning while she is at her desk. These episodes are brief, involving sudden jerks of the right upper limb with occasional face twitching and a momentary arrest in activity, without loss of awareness. She also notes occasional brief déjà vu sensations and a rising epigastric feeling preceding some events, consistent with focal-onset features.

On history, there is no recent intercurrent illness, sleep deprivation is minimal, and alcohol intake remains low. She has not missed medication doses. The temporal association with visually provocative stimuli at work is striking, and she specifically reports increased frequency when seated under LED panels that intermittently flicker and during exposure to rapidly changing on-screen graphics.

In keeping with the semiology and evolution, she has focal epilepsy. The current pattern suggests focal motor myoclonic phenomena with preserved awareness and occasional sensory auras. There have been no generalised convulsions, tongue bite, or injuries. Neurological examination today is normal between events.

We discussed practical measures. She plans, with her employer’s support, to trial relocation away from the brightest overhead panels, use glare-reduction filters and screen refresh adjustments, and increase natural light breaks. She will maintain a detailed seizure and trigger diary capturing time of day, lighting conditions, and workload to corroborate the apparent photosensitivity component.

Given the escalation to 6 to 7 myoclonic per week and the clear functional impact at work, this constitutes a deterioration from her prior baseline. I have arranged outpatient EEG with intermittent photic stimulation and hyperventilation, and will request an MRI epilepsy protocol if not already on file to ensure structural correlation is excluded. Bloods for levetiracetam levels are not routinely informative, but routine FBC/U&E/LFTs and vitamin D will be checked.

If workplace adjustments and environmental modifications do not lead to early improvement, we may need to consider treatment optimisation at the next review. She is aware of safety advice regarding operating at heights, near water, and avoiding fatigue. She does not drive.

We will see her back in eight weeks, sooner if events escalate further or if she experiences any loss of awareness or injury.

Yours sincerely

Flat 4, 16 Mill Street, London, SE1 2XR 

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. He has a confirmed diagnosis of generalised epilepsy. Since our last contact, he has implemented smartphone-based alarms and NFC tag prompts to support adherence after previously missed doses, which he reports have been helpful in keeping to his regimen.

He states that he has had five or seven seizures during the last two months. He describes these as sudden loss of awareness followed by generalised tonic–clonic activity witnessed by his partner on two occasions; on the other occasions he awoke with tongue biting and post-ictal myalgia. We discussed typical precipitants for generalised seizures including sleep loss and intercurrent illness. He links two of the recent events to a viral upper respiratory infection and one to a late night at work. He has begun using his phone’s medication log to document any missed doses and seizure times, which should improve accuracy of future reviews.

Examination today was unremarkable with no focal neurological deficits. Weight and blood pressure are stable. Recent routine bloods supplied by primary care were within expected ranges.

Plan: I have advised him to continue his current antiepileptic regimen and to maintain the alarm/NFC adherence supports, as these appear to have reduced missed doses. I have arranged an outpatient EEG to reassess generalised epileptiform activity and will review him with results in approximately three months. He will continue to record seizures and any missed doses in his app. He knows to contact us sooner if frequency escalates, if he sustains injury, or if there are concerns about medication tolerance. Yours sincerely

component_inputs.note_text:
KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr Anil Rao
Riverside Health Centre

12 Meadowbank, Southwark
London SE1 9XX
Dear Dr Anil Rao
Sophie Turner, DOB: 14-03-1989, Hospital No: H739264 NHS No. 8826405172
Flat 3, 29 Mill Wharf, Deptford, London SE8 3JL 

Diagnoses/summary: Recurrent seizures with deteriorating control; prior routine and ambulatory EEGs reported non-diagnostic. MRI brain (2017) structurally unremarkable. No established provoking metabolic cause. Co-morbid migraine without aura, intermittent.

Previous medication: Levetiracetam (behavioural adverse effects, minimal efficacy), Carbamazepine (dizziness, hyponatraemia), Sodium valproate (weight gain; discontinued), Lamotrigine (partial benefit previously), Clobazam PRN (sedation), Lacosamide (ataxia), Topiramate (cognitive slowing), Zonisamide (insomnia).

Not taken: Perampanel, Brivaracetam, Cenobamate, Rufinamide, Pregabalin, Tiagabine.

I reviewed Sophie Turner in clinic today. She attended alone and provided a detailed history corroborated by diary entries and two workplace incident reports. She describes a clear deterioration over the past fortnight with events evolving faster than previously, now predominantly occurring in bright, high-noise environments such as stage rigging areas and a metal fabrication bay on the factory floor. She notes that premonitory sensations, when present, are shorter (seconds rather than minutes), and colleagues have observed earlier onset of impaired awareness and automatisms compared with her prior pattern. She has also noted increased post-event fatigue and headaches.

Seizure frequency and pattern: Prior to this recent deterioration, this month so far she has 2 seizures; earlier two in Aug, 0 in Jul and one in Jun, over waking hours and sleep. In contrast, over the last fortnight she has had seven to nine seizures during the last two weeks, with two requiring supervision at work. No clear alcohol, sleep deprivation, or intercurrent illness triggers were identified beyond the bright, high-noise settings. No tongue biting or urinary incontinence has been reported in the recent cluster; recoveries have been slower.

Medications at review:
- Lamotrigine 100 mg morning, 150 mg evening (self-reported adherence; last level pending)
- Clobazam 10 mg at night, additional 5–10 mg PRN for clusters (used twice in the last week)
- Folic acid 5 mg daily

Adverse effects reported: daytime somnolence with PRN clobazam; otherwise tolerating current baseline regimen. Mood stable. No visual blurring or diplopia. Weight stable. No new neurological deficits between events.

Examination today: Alert and oriented, speech fluent, cranial nerves intact, no lateralising motor signs, gait normal. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable. No photoparoxysmal response provoked with simple office-based light challenge, though this is not a substitute for formal testing.

Investigations: Last MRI brain (2017) normal. Prior routine EEGs non-specific; sleep-deprived EEG (2019) without epileptiform discharges. Bloods (April 2025) normal including sodium and LFTs. New bloods (U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D) and lamotrigine level sent today; results to be copied to you.

Risk and functional impact: The escalation in frequency and acceleration of event evolution, particularly in high-stimulus workplaces, represents a clear deterioration in control with increased risk of injury. She has self-restricted tasks at height and is temporarily avoiding strobe-lit stages. She no longer drives.

Plan:
- Safety: Advised strict adherence to workplace modifications already initiated by occupational health; avoid work at height and unsupervised tasks near moving machinery until stability improves. Seizure first aid refreshed; written advice provided for employer.
- Monitoring: Provided a structured seizure diary template and asked her to record environmental exposures (light/noise levels) and sleep. Offered video capture where safe and feasible.
- Investigations: Urgent outpatient prolonged video-EEG monitoring request submitted, with photic stimulation and sound sensitivity protocols, to characterise current events given the recent deterioration. Repeat MRI brain with epilepsy protocol requested in view of change in semiology.
- Medications: No abrupt changes today given recent clustering. Will review lamotrigine level; if subtherapeutic, consider cautious dose optimisation. Should further clusters occur, advised PRN clobazam may be used as already prescribed, within agreed limits; she understands sedation risk. Alternative options discussed for future consideration (patient-informed): brivaracetam or perampanel, acknowledging prior behavioural effects with levetiracetam.
- Support: Epilepsy specialist nurse to telephone within 1–2 weeks to reassess frequency and review safety measures. Provided information on trigger management in high-stimulus environments and reasonable workplace adjustments.
- Follow-up: Rapid-access review in 6 weeks or sooner if events escalate, loss of consciousness with injury, or new neurological symptoms.

Given the recent increase to seven to nine seizures during the last two weeks, I am concerned about ongoing instability and have flagged her investigations as urgent. I will update you when results are available and will coordinate medication adjustments accordingly.

Thank you for your continued care.

Yours sincerely

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Amelia Cross
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr Amelia Cross
Consultant Neurologist,  

Daniel Reeves, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: K742019 NHS No. 2045896713  
19 Brookside Close, London, SE15 3HT

Thank you for your referral and the accompanying summary. I reviewed Daniel Reeves in clinic today. He reports a clear deterioration in his seizure control in the context of greater social pressure at work and increased alcohol exposure over the past month. Specifically, he has experienced 2 to 3 drop attacks during the last two weeks, described as abrupt loss of posture with brief unresponsiveness and rapid reorientation, though with post-event headache and myalgia lasting several hours. His partner corroborates these events and notes occasional early-morning jerks and brief staring spells on waking.

He has a prior diagnosis of generalised epilepsy, previously managed on sodium valproate with reasonable stability for over a year. He admits to missing evening doses on two occasions recently, often coinciding with social drinking. There has been no reported focal onset, aura, or lateralising features. No tongue-biting or urinary incontinence reported in the recent drop attacks. He denies prolonged confusion, but describes increased irritability and sleep disruption.

Neurological examination today was non-focal. Cardiovascular observations were within normal limits. There were no injuries from the recent drop attacks beyond mild bruising to the knees. He is not currently driving and understands the DVLA regulations.

In my view, the pattern is consistent with a deterioration of seizure control in established generalised epilepsy, likely precipitated by stress, sleep disruption, and alcohol exposure. I discussed with him the importance of strict adherence to medication and avoidance of alcohol; he acknowledges the link between recent lifestyle changes and increased events. He is amenable to a brief period of closer monitoring and further investigation if needed.

Plan discussed with the patient and partner:
- Reinforce seizure diary keeping, including timing, potential triggers (alcohol, sleep deprivation), and injuries.
- Safety advice provided for drop attacks (avoid heights, use of protective strategies at home such as shower rather than bath, caution with sharp objects). His partner is aware of basic first aid for generalised seizures.
- I have arranged repeat routine EEG to reassess interictal generalised epileptiform activity, and will proceed to ambulatory EEG if events persist. Bloods requested today (U&E, LFTs, FBC) given valproate use.
- I will review him again in 6 weeks, or sooner if there are further drop attacks, injuries, or any prolonged events.

Please let me know if you would like any further information. I will update you after the EEG and follow-up review.

Yours sincerely

He will continue his seizure diary and has been advised to inform a trusted colleague of his typical events and recovery period. Department of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Amelia Grant  
City University Hospital  
Department of Neurology, 12 Riverbank Way, Manchester M3 4QH  

Dear Dr Amelia Grant,  

Michael Davies, DOB: 14-02-1991, Hospital No: M983472 NHS No. 6045198723  
Flat 2B, 17 Copper Street, Manchester, M15 6AL 

Diagnoses: 

Recurrent episodes suggestive of focal-onset seizures with impaired awareness. MRI brain (July 2025) normal. Routine EEG (August 2025) unremarkable. 

Current Medication: 

Levetiracetam 500 mg bd 

Plan: 

- Continue Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily.  
- Provide written workplace safety advice regarding prolonged standing, heat, and crowd surges; patient to share with employer’s occupational health.  
- Maintain a regular sleep schedule and adequate hydration.  
- Report any escalation in event frequency or occurrence with loss of consciousness or injury.  
- Seizure diary to continue; follow-up in 6 months, sooner if concerns.  

I reviewed Michael Davies in clinic today. He works on the gate line at a busy metro station where prolonged standing, variable temperatures, and occasional crowd surges are routine. Over the last two months he has documented five to six focal automatisms during the last two months, typically brief (30–60 seconds) episodes of lip-smacking and right-hand picking movements, followed by several minutes of confusion and fatigue. He reports that missed meals, poor sleep after late shifts, and sensory overload at peak times may precede events. There has been no tongue biting, no witnessed generalised convulsions, and no injuries. 

He commenced Levetiracetam 500 mg twice a day in early August 2025, with initial irritability that settled after two weeks; no other adverse effects reported. Bloods including FBC, U&E and LFTs in September 2025 were within normal ranges. MRI brain and routine EEG have not identified a structural or electrophysiological correlate. 

Given the persisting brief episodes, I advised continued adherence to medication and practical risk reduction at work: avoiding solo posts during the busiest periods where feasible, ensuring access to water, and arranging short rotation breaks to mitigate prolonged standing and heat. He will continue his seizure diary and has been advised to inform a trusted colleague of his typical events and recovery period. Driving advice has been given in line with current DVLA regulations for seizures with impaired awareness; he understands the requirement to cease driving and to notify the DVLA if applicable. 

I will review him in six months, or earlier if there is any deterioration, emergence of convulsive seizures, or injury at work. 

With best wishes,

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 06 January 2020

Dr Eleanor Shah
Riverside Health Centre

12 Millbank, London SW1P 3GE
Dear Dr Eleanor Shah
Amelia Hart, DOB: 14-02-1990, Hospital No: H937451 NHS No. 8421195630
Flat 4, 26 Willow Street, London EC2A 4BH

Diagnoses/summary: Recurrent seizures of unclear classification; prior routine EEG non-diagnostic; MRI brain previously reported as normal (no structural correlate identified). Suspected catamenial pattern based on patient-reported symptom diary and menstrual tracking app entries.

Previous medication: Levetiracetam (fatigue and irritability), sodium valproate in adolescence (stopped when planning pregnancy), carbamazepine (dizziness), lamotrigine (insufficient benefit at 200 mg/day), clobazam PRN (helpful for clusters but daytime sedation). 

Not taken: topiramate, zonisamide, lacosamide, perampanel, brivaracetam, pregabalin, tiagabine, rufinamide.

Comorbidities: Migraine without aura; mild iron-deficiency anaemia under GP care. No known cardiac disease.

I reviewed Amelia Hart in clinic today. She attended alone. She reports nocturnal episodes occurring once per night on average for the past three months, typically between 02:00 and 04:00. Her partner has observed brief arousals with groaning, limb stiffening and jaw clenching lasting under a minute, followed by confusion and headache on waking. She does not recall an aura. She has used a menstrual tracking app and notes that the frequency and intensity of these episodes increase in the five days preceding menstruation and the first two days of bleeding. She shared screenshots from the app which align with a cyclical clustering pattern. Daytime events are rare and have not occurred in the last eight weeks. She denies tongue biting or urinary incontinence recently. 

She is currently not driving and is aware of DVLA guidance. Sleep is fragmented, and she reports morning fatigue and reduced concentration at work. No recent head injuries. Alcohol minimal. No illicit drug use. She is taking over-the-counter iron as advised by her GP.

Examination today was unremarkable. Vitals stable. Neurological examination normal. 

Current medication:
- Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily (patient-led reduction from 200 mg/day due to lethargy; no clear change in events)
- Folic acid 5 mg daily
- Sumatriptan 50 mg PRN for migraine (≤4 per month)

Plan:
- Ambulatory EEG (preferably including an overnight recording) to capture nocturnal events, with patient to press event marker if aware and partner to keep contemporaneous notes. 
- Request patient to continue detailed seizure and menstrual tracking via her app and to export monthly summaries for clinic review; advised to note sleep duration and stressors. 
- Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, vitamin D, ferritin; lamotrigine trough level prior to morning dose for reference only. 
- Safety: discussed nocturnal precautions (no sleeping at elevated bunk, consider padded headboard, avoid unsupervised bathing, use of seizure alarm if acceptable). Provided SUDEP and Night-time Seizure information leaflet. 
- Medication strategy to be reviewed after ambulatory EEG. We discussed options in principle, including optimising current therapy versus introducing an alternative agent, and the potential role of short-term perimenstrual adjustment if the pattern remains consistent; she prefers to wait for EEG results before any changes. Side effects and contraceptive interactions were explained in general terms. 
- Offered referral to epilepsy specialist nurse for support and to set up a telephone review in 4–6 weeks to monitor the once per night nocturnal events and overall wellbeing while investigations proceed. 
- Follow-up in clinic in 3 months or sooner if events escalate, injury occurs, or daytime episodes recur.

Thank you for your ongoing care, including management of anaemia and repeat prescriptions. Please do not hesitate to contact me if there are concerns before the next review.

Yours sincerely

Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr Fiona
Centre for Epilepsy
Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG

Dear Dr Fiona,

Susan Miller, DOB: 14-05-1986, Hospital No: P948572 NHS No. 7623549812
12 Baker Street, London, NW1 6XE

Epilepsy – Focal Epilepsy Type

Medication: Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily; Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily (patient-reported adherence, no recent changes)

Lamotrigine Blood Level:
19 September 2025: 3.2 mg/L (reference 1.0–15.0 mg/L). Dose at sampling: 100 mg twice daily

Seizures: Prior to recent deterioration, seizure frequency characterised by periods of clustering followed by quiescence. Over the past 6 weeks, there has been clear worsening with an absence seizure every night, often preceded by evening fatigue and followed by morning headache and reduced concentration. No generalised tonic–clonic seizures reported. Partner has observed brief behavioural arrest with staring and unresponsiveness lasting 10–20 seconds, sometimes with right-hand fumbling.

I reviewed Susan Miller today in clinic. She works in a care setting with irregular breaks and frequent patient transfers. She reports cumulative fatigue across shifts with perceived worsening of events and functional decline at work. She notes that previously she experienced clusters of focal impaired-awareness seizures interspersed with quiescent periods, but now describes an absence seizure every night, which marks a deterioration from her baseline. Events are more predictable in the late evening after back-to-back shifts. No new precipitants identified other than sleep disruption and physical exhaustion. No missed doses declared. No injuries reported.

Neurological examination today was non-focal. BP 118/72, pulse 72 regular. No postictal deficits. 

Plan discussed today:
- Safety counselling reinforced around nocturnal events and work fatigue management (patient to discuss rota adjustments and protected breaks with employer).
- Arrange ambulatory EEG with sleep capture to better characterise nocturnal events and confirm focal onset with secondary generalisation excluded.
- Serum Levetiracetam level to be checked with next bloods; repeat Lamotrigine level in 2–3 weeks to confirm stability.
- Sleep hygiene advice provided; patient will keep a seizure/sleep/workload diary.
- Follow-up in 6–8 weeks or sooner if escalation (injury, daytime clusters, or generalised convulsions).

I will update you once investigations are available. Please let us know if work accommodations are feasible, as cumulative fatigue appears contributory to this deterioration.

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Clinic

Neurosciences Division

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr Patel
South Thames Neurology Service
St George’s Hospital, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT

Dear Dr Patel,

James Walker, DOB: 14-07-1988, Hospital No: H629381 NHS No. 9473158620
Flat 3, 12 Meadow Lane, London SE15 4AB

Diagnoses:

Focal epilepsy.

Thank you for reviewing James Walker, who works in a manual, safety‑sensitive role involving heights and machinery. He reports ongoing focal impaired‑awareness episodes with morning predominance. Over the past four weeks he has noticed two clusters this month; each ≈five absences in the morning. He describes these as brief periods of behavioural arrest with staring, loss of track of tasks, and automatic hand movements, followed by fatigue and mild headache. There is no clear convulsion, no tongue‑bite, and no incontinence. Triggers are suspected early starts and missed breakfast on shift days.

He remains on lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily with good tolerability (no rash, dizziness, or mood change). No rescue medication has been required. He has been fully adherent and uses a phone reminder. There is no recent intercurrent illness. Sleep is irregular on rotating shifts, and caffeine intake is high on night rotations. No alcohol excess. Family note occasional brief speech arrest preceding the episodes by a few seconds.

Neurological examination today was unremarkable. Prior MRI (2023) showed a subtle left mesial temporal signal change without overt hippocampal volume loss. Routine EEG (2024) demonstrated left temporal sharp waves. These findings support a diagnosis of focal epilepsy with probable left temporal onset.

Given his safety‑critical duties, we discussed risk management at work. He understands the need to avoid tasks at height or near unguarded machinery if he experiences prodromal symptoms, and to inform occupational health. We provided written advice on sleep hygiene, regular meals, and hydration, and agreed on a seizure diary to document timing relative to shifts. We did not make medication changes today, but if clustering persists, we will consider a cautious lamotrigine increase or add‑on levetiracetam. He consents to us liaising with his employer’s occupational health team if needed.

Plan:
- Continue lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily.
- Seizure diary focusing on shift pattern and morning events; note any aura or speech arrest.
- Lifestyle measures: regular breakfast before early shifts; optimise sleep; reduce caffeine after midnight on nights.
- Occupational health advice provided; avoid working at height or with moving machinery on days with prodrome or after a morning cluster.
- Bloods today: FBC, U&E, LFTs—results to be copied to you.
- Review in 8 weeks, sooner if there is any increase beyond two clusters per month or new features (convulsions, injury).

Yours sincerely,

Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 20 November 2015 

Dr A. Rahman 
Consultant Neurologist  
Centre for Epilepsy  
King’s College Hospital, London  

Dear Dr A. Rahman, 

Mr Thomas Green, DOB: 04-09-2003, Hospital No: K847129 NHS No. 9384756102  
Flat 12, 27 Campus Road, London, SE5 9AB  

Diagnosis: 

Focal epilepsy with stress- and sleep-loss-related breakthrough events; improved consistency on Lamotrigine; Levetiracetam previously associated with irritability and discontinued

Aetiology: 

No structural lesion identified on MRI; normal perinatal and developmental history

Other Medical Problems: 

Intermittent tension-type headache; myopia corrected with lenses

Management Plan: 

Continue Lamotrigine (single brand) 200 mg twice daily. Maintain a seizure and sleep diary. I have advised timing doses strictly 12 hours apart and taking evening dose before prolonged gaming sessions. We will arrange a 24-hour ambulatory EEG if events persist beyond next review. Review in four months; check trough Lamotrigine level at that visit.

This patient is the lead of a university esports club with prolonged evening screen time and irregular sleep during tournament weeks. He reports brief focal aware seizures characterised by a rising epigastric sensation, left-hand paraesthesias, and transient word-finding difficulty lasting 30–60 seconds without loss of awareness or postictal confusion. Seizure days: six/30 this month, clustering after late-night practice sessions extending past 01:00 and on days following <5 hours of sleep. There have been no convulsions, no injuries, and no episodes while driving; he is not currently driving. Caffeine intake is moderate (2–3 energy drinks on event days). Alcohol minimal. No missed doses reported in the past month; he previously tried Levetiracetam but stopped due to mood change. We discussed non-prescriptive strategies he reports finding acceptable, including scheduling earlier scrims, using blue-light filters, and setting a device curfew to preserve sleep. No other medication changes today.

Yours sincerely

Primary generalised epilepsy

Plan of Action:

Given the clear temporal association with reduced sleep and otherwise stable control, we discussed optimising nocturnal coverage and minimising sedative burden during the day. We will maintain sodium valproate at the current dose and introduce a small evening top‑up of clobazam to improve resilience to sleep loss on higher‑risk nights identified by the carer.

Please adjust clobazam as follows: continue 10 mg at night on routine days; on evenings preceding anticipated short sleep (e.g. travel or early starts as identified by the carer), increase to 15 mg that night only. We reinforced sleep hygiene measures with the carer (consistent bedtime, limiting late caffeine, keeping the sleep environment quiet) and asked them to continue detailed logging of sleep duration and seizure activity. If seizures begin to occur despite adequate sleep, we will consider transitioning clobazam to an alternative adjunct such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam, balancing tolerability and interaction profile with valproate.

With best wishes

Department of Neurology

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr Amelia Turner
St Cuthbert’s NHS Neurology Centre
Level 3, Neurology Outpatients, St Cuthbert’s Hospital, Durham DH1 3LE

Dear Dr Amelia Turner,

Emily Carter, DOB: 14-02-1992, Hospital No: H937520 NHS No. 9065314827
Flat 12, 8 Market Street, Durham, DH1 1BP

Diagnoses:

Focal epilepsy with secondary generalisation suspected from right temporal onset.
MRI brain (2023) unremarkable.
EEG (2024) intermittent right temporal sharp waves.

Current Medication:

Levetiracetam 1 g bd
Lamotrigine 50 mg bd

Plan:

- Continue current anti-seizure medications and maintain seizure/symptom diary with specific note of menstrual cycle timing.
- Discussed perimenstrual seizure pattern; consider future perimenstrual rescue strategy if needed (patient to review after three cycles).
- Lifestyle advice reinforced: regular sleep, stress management, and avoidance of missed doses.
- Safety and SUDEP counselling undertaken; driving regulations discussed (no current restrictions as events are predictable and the patient is not driving).
- Follow-up in 6 months, sooner if seizure pattern changes.

I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today. She reports focal aware auras of rising epigastric sensation and brief speech arrest, occasionally progressing to impaired awareness. Importantly, she observes a clear and consistent catamenial pattern: Seizures happen when perimenstrual only (days -2 to +2). Outside this window she remains seizure-free. She has tracked this pattern over the last six menstrual cycles, and her partner corroborates the clustering around the perimenstrual period.

Her examination today was normal. Review of prior investigations shows an unremarkable MRI and an EEG with intermittent right temporal sharp waves, supporting a focal epilepsy diagnosis. She tolerates levetiracetam and low-dose lamotrigine without adverse effects and has had no mood disturbance. We discussed non-pharmacological measures, adherence, and the importance of continuing a detailed diary aligning events with cycle days.

Given the stable inter-cycle control and the predictable perimenstrual clustering, we agreed to continue the current regimen for now. If perimenstrual events persist with similar frequency, we will consider a targeted perimenstrual adjustment or rescue plan at the next review, guided by her diary data.

I have arranged follow-up in six months. She will contact the service sooner if there is any change in seizure semiology, frequency outside the perimenstrual window, or medication side effects.

With best wishes,

Yours sincerely,

King's College Hospital 

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 25 October 2018 

Dr Priya Menon
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr Priya Menon
Consultant Neurologist,  

Sarah Bennett, DOB: 14-03-1989, Hospital No: KCH728450 NHS No. 9475203681  
22 Brookside Close, London, SE15 8HT

Thank you for asking me to review your patient, whom I saw in clinic today, accompanied by her partner and an assistance dog in training provided through a charitable programme. She reports that her habitual events have persisted over the last year and she has begun logging them with a menstrual tracking app to better understand timing. She notes that the attacks cluster around her period, with the window of vulnerability beginning a few days prior to bleeding and extending into the early days thereafter. Outside that peri-period interval, she seldom experiences events. She describes this pattern as “most episodes falling from roughly three days before the period up to three days afterwards,” which her partner’s observations broadly corroborate.

The typical spell begins without warning, with a brief pause in activity and a blank facial expression. This is followed by loss of responsiveness and stiffening of both arms with a low vocal sound; on some occasions there is bilateral shaking lasting under two minutes. She is usually tired and mildly confused for 30–60 minutes afterwards, sometimes with headache. She denies clear nocturnal events, tongue biting or urinary incontinence, and has no consistent focal neurological symptoms pre- or post-event. She reports no recent head injury, febrile seizures in childhood, or family history of similar episodes. Sleep deprivation and marked stress may lower her threshold, but alcohol does not appear to be a trigger. She is not currently driving.

Medication history: she is taking lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily without reported rash, and folic acid 5 mg daily. She has previously tried levetiracetam for six months but discontinued due to irritability. No known drug allergies. She uses a period-tracking diary and has begun aligning her logs with her partner’s notes and smartwatch detections of elevated heart rate during events; these data suggest the cyclical clustering described above.

Examination in clinic today was unremarkable with normal cranial nerves, tone, power, coordination and gait. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were normal. There were no signs of depression on brief screen, though she describes intermittent anxiety around the time of anticipated episodes. The assistance dog in training remained calm and did not interfere with the assessment; she reports the dog has been conditioned to alert her partner when she becomes unresponsive, which has improved safety at home.

Prior investigations: routine EEG six months ago was within normal limits. MRI brain (1.5T) last year was reported as structurally normal. Bloods including U&E, LFT, glucose, thyroid function and prolactin (post-event sampling not obtained) have been unremarkable. Cycle tracking notes were shown on her phone and suggest the temporal clustering stated above.

Impression: ongoing recurrent events with a clear temporal association to the menstrual cycle as described. At present I cannot provide a single unifying classification of the events from the information available. The pattern and witness accounts warrant further characterisation.

Plan:
- I have requested ambulatory EEG with event button capture timed across the late luteal to early follicular phase next cycle, as she reliably experiences events within that interval. 
- Repeat high-resolution MRI brain (3T) with epilepsy protocol to be arranged.
- Continue lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily for now; she prefers to avoid changes until after the monitoring period. She understands the importance of strict adherence and will continue to log events.
- Safety advice reinforced: avoid baths unsupervised, consider showering with door unlocked, caution with heights and open water, and continue partner supervision during higher-risk days as per her log. The assistance dog training team will be informed (with her consent) of monitoring dates so they can support exposure in a controlled manner.
- I have provided a seizure first aid leaflet and discussed SUDEP risk in simple terms; she is aware of the benefit of regular sleep and stress management.
- We discussed that if the cyclical pattern is consistently demonstrated on monitoring, we could explore time-targeted strategies in liaison with her GP and gynaecology colleagues.

I will review her in clinic after the ambulatory EEG and MRI are completed. Please let me know if I can provide any further information. Thank you again for involving me in her care.

Yours sincerely

component_inputs.note_text:
Epilepsy Centre 

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Patel  
North Thames Neurology Service  
Outpatient Department, Riverside Health Centre, London, W6 2JL  

Dear Dr Patel,  

Maya Johnson, DOB: 14-07-2010, Hospital No: H529317 NHS No. 9482103576  
12 Brookside Close, London, W4 1AB  

Diagnoses: 

Seizure disorder under ongoing evaluation. 

I reviewed Maya Johnson in clinic today with her mother. She remains on a ketogenic/modified diet programme that is being supervised by a paediatric metabolic team elsewhere; diet details were recorded in our notes for reference. She reports good adherence to the prescribed carbohydrate ratio and maintains a stable weight with no reported gastrointestinal adverse effects. Home blood ketone logs were shown and appear within the target range documented by the external team.

Since her last neurology review, medication was adjusted by the referring team with a modest dose increase of her maintenance antiseizure medicine four weeks ago. In the month following that change, she and her mother have noticed that the overall pattern of events has shifted: Frequency increased by ~20% after dose increase. Events remain brief, typically seconds to under a minute, with preserved awareness in some but not all instances; there has been no associated injury, and there is no new focal neurological deficit reported. She denies medication side effects beyond mild morning fatigue over the past fortnight.

There have been no emergency department attendances, no use of rescue medication, and no status events. Triggers continue to include poor sleep and intercurrent illness as previously described. A seizure diary was reviewed and corroborates the above pattern.

On examination today, general and neurological examinations were unremarkable. Vital signs were stable. No cutaneous stigmata or focal signs were elicited. 

Investigations: No new imaging since last MRI (unchanged). Prior EEGs remain non-diagnostic with non-specific changes. Routine bloods last month were within reference limits, including bicarbonate and lipid profile as monitored for dietary therapy.

Plan: 
- We will collate and share today’s seizure frequency data and the diet log with the supervising dietary team to ensure coordinated care. 
- No immediate medication changes were made today; we will seek clarification from the referring prescriber regarding the rationale for the recent dose increase given the reported change in frequency. 
- Safety advice and seizure first aid were reinforced. She will continue the seizure diary and bring home ketone readings to the next review. 
- We will arrange a follow-up in 8–10 weeks, or sooner if there is any escalation in event duration, clustering, injury, or concerns from the family or school. 

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Centre 

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Patel  
Northern General Hospital  
Department of Neurology, Herries Road, Sheffield S5 7AU  

Dear Dr Patel,  

James Walker, DOB: 14-08-1990, Hospital No: S947213 NHS No. 8035162947  
12 Millstone Close, Sheffield, S6 2QP  

Diagnoses: 

Generalised epilepsy. 

Thank you for asking me to review James Walker in the neurology clinic. He attended alone today and works in a manual, safety‑sensitive role involving heights and intermittent use of powered machinery. He remains on sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 1 g twice daily. Three weeks ago his GP increased levetiracetam to 1.25 g twice daily following two brief morning absences at work. Since that change, James Walker reports that his typical events remain generalised tonic‑clonic seizures occurring predominantly from sleep, with occasional brief absence episodes during the day. He keeps a diary and notes: "Frequency increased by ~20% after dose increase." This has been over a 3‑week observation window and coincided with a run of night shifts. No injuries reported, but one witnessed near‑miss on a gantry when he felt pre‑syncopal and stepped back as a precaution. There is no new head injury, systemic illness, or missed doses. Sleep deprivation is likely contributory. No rescue medication used. 

On examination today he was well, cardiorespiratory exam normal, and neurological examination unremarkable between events. Weight 82 kg, BP 124/76, pulse 72 regular. No tremor or ataxia. 

Investigations: Routine bloods (FBC, U&Es, LFTs) last week were within normal limits. Levetiracetam level not measured; valproate level mid‑therapeutic range per GP record. Prior MRI brain (2022) normal. EEG (2023) showed generalised spike‑and‑wave discharges consistent with generalised epilepsy. 

Plan discussed with James Walker: He will continue his current prescribed regimen for now while we clarify whether the observed increase is a transient fluctuation related to shift pattern and sleep loss. He will maintain a detailed seizure/symptom diary including sleep hours, shifts worked, and any near‑misses. We have arranged an urgent occupational health review through his employer regarding task allocation around heights and machinery. I have requested a trough levetiracetam level before morning dose in two weeks, alongside repeat LFTs. We will bring forward his routine EEG to assess for any change in interictal activity and schedule a telephone review in three weeks to reassess frequency and tolerability. He understands DVLA guidance remains applicable as previously advised. 

Safety: We discussed practical risk reduction at work and at home, including ensuring colleagues are aware of basic first aid for seizures, avoiding lone working at height, and using fall‑arrest where mandated by site policy. He carries an ID card and has consented to me copying this letter to occupational health. 

I will keep you updated and would be happy to review sooner if there are further events or concerns. 

Yours sincerely

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 21 September 2025 

Dr Patel
Riverside Health Centre

12 Riverside Way, London, SE1 6AB
Dear Dr Patel
Jane Smith, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: H392847 NHS No. 7748291930
Flat 4, 28 Mill Street, London, SE1 2BQ 

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. Since their last appointment, there has been a notable worsening in their overall seizure control. The patient reports increasing unpredictability and more disruptive episodes, particularly clustered around the perimenstrual period, raising concern for a catamenial pattern contributing to this deterioration. Despite adherence, they feel less stable day-to-day and more fatigued post-events.

They are currently taking Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily and Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily. They report no clear medication side effects aside from intermittent dizziness and increased tiredness, which they associate with the recent escalation in events. We reviewed safety measures and potential triggers; sleep disruption and premenstrual symptoms were highlighted by the patient as potential exacerbating factors.

Regarding seizure counts, the patient is unable to provide a reliable number at present due to variable frequency and unclear recalls, particularly around the perimenstrual window. They will commence a structured diary with menstrual tracking to help clarify patterns and guide management.

Given the evident deterioration and suspected hormonal influence, I have arranged:
- Urgent ambulatory EEG within the next 4–6 weeks.
- Bloods including AED levels, FBC, U&Es, LFTs, and vitamin D.
- Referral to the epilepsy specialist nurse for counselling on cycle-linked strategies and adherence support.
- Provision of an updated seizure action plan and advice on rescue medication use if appropriate after EEG review.

I will review the patient in 8–10 weeks with EEG results and diary data to consider targeted adjustments. In the interim, we discussed avoidance of sleep deprivation, alcohol moderation, and maintaining a consistent medication schedule. The patient understands the plan and knows to contact the service if there is any further deterioration, injury, or prolonged events.

Yours sincerely

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Priya Shah  
St George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust  
Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT  

Dear Dr Priya Shah,  

Jacob Reynolds, DOB: 14-11-1987, Hospital No: H392774 NHS No. 9473162058  
82 Larkspur Close, Croydon, CR0 4AN  

Diagnoses: 

Seizure disorder, aetiology under investigation. 

I reviewed Jacob Reynolds in clinic today accompanied by his partner. He reports intermittent episodes consistent with generalised convulsive seizures occurring without a clear warning. Over the last three months he has tracked events in a diary and describes TC six/mo, with post‑ictal confusion and myalgia lasting several hours. There have been no known triggers identified, though poor sleep appears to precede some events. No injuries have been reported in the last month. He has not required emergency rescue medication since August. 

Current medication: levetiracetam 1 g twice daily, vitamin D supplementation. He reports mild irritability since dose escalation but prefers to continue for now. No other neurological symptoms reported. 

Investigations: MRI brain (May 2025) reported as structurally normal. Routine EEG (June 2025) showed non‑specific findings without definite epileptiform activity. Bloods (September 2025): U&E, LFT, FBC within reference ranges. 

Plan discussed and agreed with the patient: 
- Continue levetiracetam at current dose for the time being; monitor mood and sleep.  
- Seizure diary to be maintained with exact timings and any potential precipitants.  
- Arrange sleep‑deprived EEG within the next 8 weeks.  
- Provide updated seizure first‑aid advice and safety precautions for bathing, heights, and machinery; patient acknowledges understanding.  
- DVLA guidance reiterated; patient reports he has already ceased driving.  
- Review in clinic in three months, or earlier if frequency increases or adverse effects occur. 

Yours sincerely

Occupational health at his employer has been providing periodic summaries, which he brought to clinic; these corroborate his own seizure diary entries and note frequent short episodes at work with occasional post-event confusion. In line with his diary, we documented the current frequency as TC *5/wk, with several being witnessed by colleagues. He has arranged adjustments with his employer to avoid lone working on machinery, and the occupational health summaries document these accommodations as effective in reducing injury risk, though not event frequency.

On examination today he was alert and oriented with normal cranial nerves, power, coordination and gait. No tongue lacerations were visible, and there were faint bruises over the right forearm consistent with recent falls. Routine bloods in August were unremarkable (U&E, LFTs, FBC within reference). He has not yet had prolonged EEG or video telemetry. He remains understandably anxious about work attendance and job security but declined formal counselling today; he would consider this if symptoms persist.

Plan: I have requested an expedited prolonged EEG with video monitoring to better characterise events and to align with the collateral reports from occupational health. I will also arrange a medication level check for Lamotrigine to ensure therapeutic range, although clinical correlation will guide decisions. Pending these investigations, I have not altered his current regimen. He will continue to record events and bring both his diary and any updated occupational health summaries to the next review. We discussed seizure first aid and workplace safety; he is aware to seek urgent care for prolonged events or injury.

I will write again when the investigations are available. Please let me know if there are any concerns from your side or if further workplace documentation is required.

Yours sincerely

St Mary's Hospital 

Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 12 September 2025 

Dr Ahmed  
Riverside Medical Practice  
12 Wharf Road, London N1 7SZ  

Dear Dr Ahmed,  

Sophie Miller, DOB: 04-02-1992, Hospital No: H384920 NHS No. 9054731186  
Flat 3, 22 Brookside Street, London, SE15 4JP 

Medication: 

Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily. Previously noted adverse effects to antiseizure therapies documented historically, including rash and gastrointestinal upset. No current adverse effects reported with present regimen. 

Since the last review she describes intermittent episodes of brief loss of awareness with rapid recovery and occasional tongue soreness on waking. She reports that her typical convulsive events are infrequent; she estimates TC Xnine/yr based on entries in her symptom diary and partner observations. A recent work rota change with earlier starts appears to have coincided with two nocturnal events in the past quarter, though she feels daytime functioning remains satisfactory. 

She has maintained good adherence and has introduced a consistent sleep schedule over the past month, which she feels has helped. She denies new neurological symptoms, injuries, or emergency attendances. There has been no clear trigger apart from the shift pattern, and alcohol intake remains minimal. 

Given the historically recorded sensitivity to several antiseizure medications with rash and gastrointestinal upset, she is keen to avoid changes at present. We discussed general measures around sleep regularity and recording of spells; she will continue to use her diary and share copies with us before the next visit. 

I have arranged routine bloods (U&E, LFTs) locally via your practice and will review the results when available. She is content with the current plan and knows to contact us sooner if frequency increases, injuries occur, or if there are any concerns. 

We will see her again in four months. 

Yours sincerely

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr A. Malik
Riverside Health Centre

12 Stonebridge Way
Southwark
London SE1 5JT
Dear Dr A. Malik
Jordan Ellis, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: H927451 NHS No. 8439201756
Flat 3, 28 Wharf Street, London SE8 4DN 

Diagnoses/summary: Recurrent unprovoked seizures with ongoing events; prior routine EEG reported as non-diagnostic; brain MRI (2023) structurally normal; ongoing occupational risk due to warehouse duties between tall racking and narrow aisles

Previous medication: Levetiracetam (behavioural irritability), Lamotrigine (rash after titration), Carbamazepine (dizziness), Sodium valproate (weight gain, tremor), Lacosamide (no clear benefit), Clobazam PRN (sedation)

Not taken: Topiramate, Zonisamide, Perampanel, Brivaracetam, Rufinamide, Pregabalin, Tiagabine

Occupational context: Works as a warehouse picker in narrow aisles between tall racking; shift patterns vary with differing lifting demands and pace. Reports that rushing during late shifts increases stress and poor sleep. Has used a voice-activated headset for picking which is sometimes disorientating during post-event confusion.

I reviewed Jordan Ellis in clinic today. They attended alone. They report ongoing brief losses of awareness with sudden behavioural arrest and occasional falls. Frequency currently described as "sz x3/d" on their seizure diary, with clustering on late shifts. They note pre-event sensations of light-headedness, ringing in the ears, and a rising nausea on some days, but at other times events occur without warning. Post-event fatigue lasts 20–40 minutes. No tongue-biting or urinary incontinence reported recently. A witness at work described staring, dropping the handheld scanner, and a slow return to baseline. No clear alcohol excess; caffeine 2–3 cups/day. Sleep fragmented on rotating shifts.

Investigations: Routine EEG (2024) non-diagnostic; no interictal epileptiform activity captured. MRI brain (2023) reported no focal cortical abnormalities. Bloods (Aug 2025): FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT within reference range; vitamin D low–normal. No known head injury. No family history of epilepsy reported.

Current medication:
- Brivaracetam 50 mg twice daily (initiated by prior team; modest reduction in duration but not frequency)
- Folic acid 5 mg daily (precautionary)
- Omeprazole 20 mg daily (dyspepsia)

Adverse effects: Reports occasional low mood and reduced motivation since starting brivaracetam; denies suicidality. No visual symptoms or rash.

Functional/safety considerations: Given the warehouse role between tall racking and narrow aisles, we discussed immediate safety measures: stepping away from elevated pallets when feeling unwell, informing a supervisor of ongoing events, and avoiding climbing or working at height. They do not operate forklifts. Has a personal alarm badge but not consistently used.

Plan:
- Continue brivaracetam 50 mg twice daily for now. I have provided written information and discussed potential titration options at follow-up depending on tolerability and effect.
- Arrange ambulatory EEG (48–72 hours) aiming to capture typical events, timed across two shift patterns if possible.
- Repeat bloods including vitamin D and brivaracetam level (baseline) before any dose change.
- Seizure diary to continue; patient to record shift type, sleep duration, and any missed meals alongside event times to correlate with "sz x3/d" entries.
- Occupational advice letter (separate) to employer recommending avoidance of tasks at height and working alone in narrow aisles until better control is achieved; encourage buddy system during late shifts.
- Lifestyle measures discussed: sleep regularity where feasible, hydration, and pacing during high-demand shifts; patient to trial pre-shift snack to mitigate light-headedness.
- DVLA guidance reiterated; patient confirms they are not driving.
- Follow-up in 8–10 weeks, sooner if deterioration or adverse effects. If ambulatory EEG captures typical events, we will review therapeutic options including alternative agents not yet tried.

Thank you for your ongoing care and prescription support. Please let me know if you or the patient have any concerns before the next appointment.

Yours sincerely

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr Ayesha Rahman
Southside Health Centre

12 Brook Lane, London SE15 3QT
Dear Dr Ayesha Rahman
Amelia Carter, DOB: 14-03-1996, Hospital No: H928417 NHS No. 8035619240
Flat 3, 29 Alder Grove, London SE23 2LP 

Diagnoses/summary: Generalised epilepsy with catamenial pattern suspected; patient-reported clustering around menses. Long-standing history of absence and generalised tonic–clonic seizures (GTCs). Previous EEGs demonstrating generalised spike–wave discharges; no focal onset features elicited. 

Neuroimaging: MRI brain (2021) structurally normal, no focal cortical dysplasia or mesial temporal sclerosis identified.

Seizure burden: As per diary and menstrual tracking app entries, sz Xfour/wk on average over the last 8 weeks, with clear peri-menstrual exacerbation (days −3 to +3). Occasional early-morning myoclonic jerks reported. No recent injuries; one tongue bite last month; no prolonged post-ictal confusion beyond 20–30 minutes. 

Safety/social: Not driving. No current pregnancies. Uses period-tracking app (patient consented to share summary logs) showing cycles 28–31 days; seizure clusters align with luteal–perimenstrual window. Sleep disruption and stress noted as additional triggers.

Current medication: 
- Sodium valproate MR 500 mg twice daily (weight neutral to +1 kg; notes mild hair change and tremor; contraception discussed previously)
- Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily (mood irritability manageable)
- Folic Acid 5 mg daily
- PRN buccal midazolam supplied but not used in past 6 months

Previous medication: Lamotrigine (breakthrough GTCs and rash), Topiramate (word-finding difficulty, paresthesias), Zonisamide (insomnia, anorexia), Clobazam (sedation), Ethosuximide (partial benefit for absences only), Perampanel (mood lability). 

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Background today: I reviewed Amelia Carter in clinic, who attended alone. She describes increasing seizure clustering around menstruation over the past 3 cycles, corroborated by her app screenshots. Fatigue and low mood premenstrually. She is otherwise well; no intercurrent infections. Sleep averaged 6 hours/night due to shift work. She denies alcohol or recreational drugs. She queries non-hormonal strategies and whether cycle-linked dose adjustments could help. She is aware of pregnancy considerations with valproate and confirms effective contraception in place. 

Examination: General and neurological examination normal between seizures. Weight 67 kg, BP 112/68. No cognitive slowing on casual testing; speech fluent. 

Discussion: We discussed that she has generalised epilepsy with probable catamenial modulation. The options covered included lifestyle optimisation (sleep regularity, stress reduction), short-cycle benzodiazepine bridging, or targeted dose adjustments around the high-risk window. We also touched on hormonal strategies via Gynaecology, noting risks/benefits. She prefers to try non-hormonal measures first, with careful monitoring. Side-effects, SUDEP information, safety around water/heights/cooking, and rescue plan were reiterated. 

Plan:
- Continue sodium valproate MR 500 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily for now. 
- Trial short intermittent clobazam 10 mg nocte from day −3 to +3 of menses for two cycles, if tolerated; counselled on sedation and driving restrictions (not currently driving). 
- Sleep hygiene measures; advise consistent bed/wake times even on shift days, consider rota discussion with employer if feasible.
- Continue folic acid 5 mg daily. Contraception to remain effective; avoid pregnancy on current regimen; preconception counselling offered when appropriate. 
- Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFTs, valproate trough level in 2 weeks; thyroid function given fatigue.
- Provide fit note if clusters interfere with work; patient to keep detailed seizure–cycle diary in the app and share PDFs prior to next review.
- Rescue plan: midazolam buccal as previously instructed for any convulsive seizure >5 minutes or seizure clusters as per plan; partner aware. 
- Refer to Gynaecology for discussion of hormonal options if inadequate response to intermittent strategy. 
- Follow-up: nurse specialist telephone review in 6 weeks to assess tolerability and impact on seizure clustering; face-to-face review in 4 months, sooner if deterioration. 

Additional notes: We confirmed safeguarding and home safety measures. She understands to seek urgent care for prolonged seizures or significant increase in frequency beyond her baseline sz Xfour/wk. She consented to the plan and data sharing of app summaries within her record. Some entries showed "Ã‚Â·" and "â€“" garbled symbols in exported text, but dates and counts were clear. 

Yours sincerely

component_inputs.note_text:
Department of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Emily Carter  
St. Mary’s Hospital  
Department of Neurology, Praed Street, London W2 1NY  

Dear Dr Emily Carter,  

Alex Turner, DOB: 14-03-2006, Hospital No: H293847 NHS No. 9845612370  
21 Brookfield Avenue, London, N10 2QJ 

Diagnoses: 

Recurrent unprovoked seizures, onset in childhood; aetiology and epilepsy classification not established. MRI brain (2023) unremarkable. Routine EEG (2024) non-specific findings without clear epileptiform activity. 

Current Medication: 

Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily  
Midazolam 10 mg buccal, as rescue for prolonged events (>5 minutes) 

Plan: 

- Continue levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily.  
- Provide written seizure action plan to patient and parent.  
- Arrange sleep-deprived EEG and repeat serum levels in 3 months.  
- Safety and lifestyle guidance reviewed (sleep hygiene, alcohol moderation, swimming with supervision).  
- Follow-up in adult epilepsy clinic in 6 months, sooner if breakthrough events increase. 

I reviewed Alex Turner in the adult neurology clinic following transition from paediatric services. They attended with a parent, who contributed collateral history. Since moving to adult care earlier this year, they report brief “blanking” spells occurring several times per week, described as short periods of unresponsiveness with loss of conversation thread and a rapid return to baseline, without motor features or post-event confusion. The parent has witnessed some of these episodes and notes that they tend to cluster when the patient is sleep-deprived or under exam stress. There have been no prolonged convulsions in the past 12 months. The patient keeps a seizure diary that records these events as occurring on most weeks, with occasional weeks free. Medication adherence is reported as good, with no significant adverse effects beyond mild irritability that has improved with dose timing adjustments. 

Neurological examination today was normal. Prior investigations include a structurally normal MRI brain (2023) and a routine EEG (2024) showing non-specific slowing without clear epileptiform discharges. In view of the ongoing brief events several times each week and the potential influence of sleep deprivation, I have arranged a sleep-deprived EEG to increase diagnostic yield. We discussed the possibility of a future medication adjustment depending on EEG findings and diary trends; for now, I have advised continuing levetiracetam at the current dose and maintaining the seizure diary. A rescue buccal midazolam plan remains in place for any prolonged event lasting more than 5 minutes, although this has not been required over the last year. 

We reviewed lifestyle and safety considerations, including regular sleep, avoidance of binge drinking, and supervised swimming. The parent is welcome to attend future appointments to provide further collateral history when available. I will see Alex Turner again in six months, with interim review if there is an increase in the frequency or severity of events. 

With best wishes,

Dear Dr Sarah Ahmed
Michael Carter, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: M837462 NHS No. 7845129630
12B Haverstock Close, London, E14 2PQ

He describes recurring episodes since adolescence with preserved awareness in some events and collapse with shaking in others, but with variable semiology and no consistent focal features reported by witnesses. He has a remote history of mild traumatic brain injury in his early 20s without documented loss of consciousness beyond a few minutes and no neurosurgical intervention. 

Since his last community review six months ago, he reports clusters of brief warning sensations (described as a rising internal feeling and metallic taste) on some days, and a smaller number of longer events with loss of awareness. He estimates the more disruptive events occur q2 - 3wk, often later in the evening, sometimes after poor sleep. There is no consistent relation to alcohol intake, and he does not drive. Post-event confusion lasts 10–20 minutes, with fatigue into the following day. There have been no tongue bites or significant injuries in the last year, though he notes occasional myalgia afterwards. Family videos are inconclusive due to partial view and low light.

Examination today was unremarkable with no lateralising neurological signs. Routine bloods last month (FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, vitamin D) were within reference limits. Interictal EEG in 2022 showed rare non-specific slowing without epileptiform discharges. 

Plan: Given the reported frequency of more disruptive events at approximately q2 - 3wk and the historical variability in semiology, I have arranged ambulatory EEG with home video capture to improve event-characterisation. For now, I have not altered medication pending these results. We discussed sleep hygiene, stress management strategies (patient-led), and the value of witness recordings when safe. He is aware of safety precautions regarding bathing, cooking with open flames, and working at heights. 

I will see him again in three months or sooner if the ambulatory EEG captures typical events earlier. He knows to contact the service if frequency increases beyond the current q2 - 3wk pattern or if new features emerge such as prolonged confusion, focal neurological deficits, or injury. 

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Centre

Neurosciences Division


From: Dr Emma Richardson (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Sent: 15 April 2020 10:15
To: neuro.epilepsy@kch.nhs.uk
Cc: Dr Michael Ahmed (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Priya Desai (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Subject: Worsening seizure control and management plan

Hi Emma

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Not specified in records; classification remains under review.

Present Medication:

1. Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily
2. Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily

Present Seizure Frequency:

Previously: Quarterly clusters with three – four convulsions per episode.
Currently: Escalation over the last six weeks with events occurring qone to twod on workdays, often clustering late afternoon; patient reports near-daily auras (brief déjà vu, nausea) and three witnessed convulsions in the past 10 days.

Clinical Summary and Context:

The patient reports an intense workload with extended hours and compressed deadlines. Events tend to cluster on workdays per patient report, particularly after consecutive late finishes. There is no clear intercurrent illness, sleep has been reduced to 5–6 hours, and caffeine intake has increased. No missed doses admitted, though one delayed evening dose last week. No new head injury, alcohol or recreational drug use reported. Collateral from partner confirms prolonged postictal confusion and one episode with tongue biting and myalgia suggestive of generalised convulsion; however, semiology has been mixed and remains non-localising, hence classification not established at present.

Plan of Action:

- Urgent optimisation: Increase levetiracetam from 750 mg to 1,000 mg twice daily for one week, then to 1,250 mg twice daily if tolerated. Maintain lamotrigine at 150 mg twice daily for now; levels to be checked in two weeks alongside U&E, LFTs, FBC.
- Rescue medication: Prescribe buccal midazolam 10 mg for convulsions lasting >5 minutes or repeated convulsions without recovery; partner to be instructed on use.
- Safety: Advise immediate cessation of driving and high-risk activities (heights, open water, operating machinery). Provide written seizure first-aid guidance.
- Triggers and lifestyle: Patient-reported workload appears contributory. Recommend temporary workload adjustments and structured sleep schedule; provide fit note for employer for four weeks to facilitate reduced hours and recovery days after events.
- Diagnostics: Arrange urgent ambulatory EEG (48–72 hours) and repeat MRI brain epilepsy protocol; review prior imaging and EEG. Seizure diary to document timing, potential triggers, and any aura.
- Follow-up: Rapid access review in three weeks or sooner if further convulsions occur. If events persist despite the above, we will discuss admission for video-EEG monitoring and consider alternative antiseizure medication.

Overall, the patient’s condition is deteriorating, with transition from previously intermittent quarterly clusters to qone to twod occurrence on workdays and increased convulsive burden. The above measures aim to stabilise control while we clarify classification and optimise therapy.

With best wishes

He describes two patterns. The first comprises brief unresponsiveness with rocking movements and vocalisation, followed by prolonged confusion lasting up to an hour. These have been present for many years. He recalls that after starting brivaracetam some time ago, the interval between events lengthened; at present, he and his partner estimate they occur every two to three weeks. The second pattern involves sudden tearfulness and marked emotionality without clear loss of awareness; these episodes have been noted by his partner and appear to cluster. He and his partner also report events occurring predominantly when settling for the night, with episodes tending to happen around bedtime and in the early hours. Yours sincerely

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 2 August 2022 

Dr Patel  
St George's Hospital  
Department of Neurology, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT  

Dear Dr Patel,  

Michael Turner, DOB: 14-11-1988, Hospital No: H527391 NHS No. 9081764523  
52 Willowbank Close, London, SW12 0AA  

Diagnoses: 

Seizure disorder (aetiology not established).

Since our last contact, he has implemented smartphone alarm schedules (morning and evening) and set up NFC tags at his bedside and kitchen to confirm dose administration; the phone records a timestamp when the tag is tapped. He feels this has improved consistency, and his partner has visibility of adherence via the shared app. There have been no adverse effects reported from medication and no new neurological symptoms. 

Seizure record (patient-reported and cross-checked with his app timestamps): Seizure: 2022: Jan x1, Feb x0, Mar x1, Apr x2, May x1, Jun x1, Jul x1. He notes typical events are brief with preserved awareness at onset, a déjà vu sensation, metallic taste, and occasional right-hand fumbling; duration under two minutes, followed by mild fatigue. No injuries, no emergency attendances. There is no clear photic sensitivity. Sleep disruption and missed doses were the most consistent antecedents before the alarm/NFC system was introduced. 

Medication: Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily. Adherence since mid-April has been high per app logs (missed or delayed doses now rare); he has enabled a 30-minute escalation alarm to his partner. Concomitants: vitamin D supplement only. He denies mood change beyond transient irritability in the first week of therapy, now resolved. 

Examination today was non-focal. Vitals within normal limits. No tremor, coordination intact, gait stable. 

Investigations: Prior MRI brain (2021) reported as normal. Prior routine EEG (2021) non-specific without definite epileptiform discharges. We discussed the option of sleep-deprived EEG if breakthrough events increase, though at present he prefers to continue observation. 

Management and plan: 
- Continue current medication dose; no changes made today. 
- Persist with smartphone alarms and NFC tap confirmation; his app analytics suggest adherence >95% since implementation. 
- Safety: no driving until legally eligible; he confirms he is currently not driving. Workplace has been informed; he avoids lone work at heights. 
- If seizure clusters recur or events generalise, he will contact us via the advice line; we would then consider ambulatory EEG and serum level check. 
- Follow-up in 4–6 months, sooner if required. 

Additional notes: He reports that the NFC tags occasionally fail to register if the phone case is misaligned; he has repositioned the tags and set a secondary alarm as backup. He and his partner find the shared log reassuring. There have been no emergency rescue medications used. 

Yours sincerely

Clinic Date: 27 November 2016 

Dr Wang
Saffron Park Hospital

Saffron Park, London, E14 7JL
Dear Dr Wang
John Doe, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: P546484 NHS No. 5484656746
Flat 15 Roundwood Road, London, E14 7JL 

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. He has a known diagnosis of focal epilepsy and continues to self-monitor carefully using a paper seizure calendar, which he brings to each appointment. He reports no recent head injuries, medication non-adherence, or sleep deprivation beyond occasional broken sleep related to shift work.

Since I last saw him in May 2016, he has kept an updated paper log. Seizure: 2016: May x1, Jun x1, Jul x0, Aug x1, Sep x0, Oct x1, Nov x0. He describes his typical events as focal aware seizures with a rising epigastric sensation and brief speech arrest lasting 30–60 seconds, without loss of awareness, followed occasionally (approximately once every 2–3 months) by focal impaired-awareness episodes with automatisms and post-event fatigue for up to an hour. He denies any generalised convulsions this year.

Current treatment: Carbamazepine modified-release 400 mg b.d. and Levetiracetam 1000 mg b.d. He reports good adherence, no rash, no diplopia, and only mild intermittent dizziness when dehydrated. No mood deterioration on Levetiracetam by his account. He does not drive and remains compliant with DVLA guidance.

Examination today was unremarkable. Neurological examination was normal with no focal deficits. Weight and blood pressure stable. Routine bloods from September 2016 (U&E, LFT, FBC) were within normal limits. He brings his original paper calendars, which corroborate the above frequency and provide consistent timing patterns (late evening predominance on days following consecutive night shifts).

Plan: Given the relative stability with focal seizures largely brief and aware, and no generalised events, I have not altered medication today. We discussed sleep hygiene and maintaining consistent dosing times. He will continue to use his paper seizure calendar and bring this to follow-up. I have requested a repeat Carbamazepine level and routine bloods via your surgery in 8–10 weeks, mainly for monitoring. If the frequency increases (two or more focal impaired-awareness events in a month) he will contact the clinic for earlier review.

I will review him again in six months, sooner if needed.

Yours sincerely

Michael Turner, DOB: 14-02-1990, Hospital No: L937521 NHS No. 9064157823  
12 Brookside Close, London, SE15 3JP 

Diagnoses: 

- Combined generalised and focal epilepsy (patient has both generalised and focal epilepsy)

- Levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily  
- Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily

- Optimise rescue plan and provide written safety leaflet; liaise with community epilepsy specialist nurse  
- Seizure diary app data to be exported to EHR and used to guide treatment adjustments  
- DVLA advice reinforced: must not drive and to notify DVLA  

I reviewed Michael Turner in my clinic today, accompanied by his partner. He uses a seizure diary app which syncs with his wearable; the entries were reviewed during the consultation. Over the last seven days the diary documents nineteen episode of status epilepticus in the past week, each defined in the app by continuous convulsive activity exceeding five minutes or repeated focal-to-bilateral tonic–clonic events without full recovery. Several events began with a focal impaired-awareness semiology (right facial twitching, speech arrest, manual automatisms) progressing to generalised tonic–clonic seizures. There were also brief absence-like events recorded on two mornings. Triggers noted by the patient include sleep deprivation and a recent viral illness. Medication adherence is reported as high, with app reminders confirming on-time dosing for the past month. Buccal midazolam was administered three times at home per the rescue plan, with partial effect.

This pattern is consistent with combined generalised and focal epilepsy, supported by prior EEG findings of generalised spike–wave activity alongside left temporal sharp waves, and MRI evidence of left mesial temporal sclerosis. Given the recent escalation, breakthrough clusters, and prolonged seizures despite dual therapy, I consider him unstable for outpatient management and have arranged urgent admission via the Same Day Emergency Care pathway for monitoring, intravenous therapy as needed, anti-seizure medication optimisation, and review of precipitating factors (infection screen, metabolic profile, and consideration of status protocol). The inpatient team will upload the last 30 days of seizure diary app logs to the record to assist titration and timing of dosing.

We discussed safety: supervision when bathing, avoiding heights and open water, adherence to the rescue protocol, and ensuring midazolam is in-date and immediately accessible. I advised strict sleep hygiene and infection management. Driving restrictions were explained; he understands that he must not drive and must inform the DVLA. Occupational and social support will be coordinated through the epilepsy specialist nurse. I will arrange a multidisciplinary review following discharge to consider longer-term options including valproate-based therapy if tolerated, and, depending on response, possible evaluation for epilepsy surgery or neuromodulation given the focal onset component.

I will update you following his inpatient stay. Please contact me if further information is required.

With best wishes,

He is known to have a history of childhood febrile seizures, with no documented events in adolescence, and has presented in adulthood with recurrent seizures. Given the clustering this week and attendance to ED, we discussed emergency care planning, medication adherence, and avoidance of sleep deprivation.
